questions.concept: GIPS: composites, who may claim compliance, firm definition, requirements
questions.stem: Halden Capital, a GIPS-compliant firm, manages a “Nordic Small-Cap” composite. In March, the portfolio manager moves a discretionary, fee-paying account out of this composite and into the firm’s “European Core” composite because the account lagged the Nordic Small-Cap composite in the previous quarter. The client’s investment guidelines have not changed and neither composite definition has been revised. The move is:

options.A: permitted, because the firm has discretion to decide which composite best fits an account’s strategy.
options.B: permitted, as long as the move is disclosed in the compliant presentations of both composites.
options.C: not permitted, because a portfolio may be moved between composites only after a documented change in the client’s guidelines or a redefinition of a composite.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Firm discretion is limited by the GIPS requirement that composites be defined by strategy and that moves be justified by documented guideline changes, not by performance.

B is incorrect. Disclosure does not cure the problem. The restriction is on the move itself, and the account’s history must stay in the original composite.

C is correct. Under GIPS, portfolios must not be switched from one composite to another unless there is a documented, significant change in the client’s investment guidelines or the composite itself is redefined. Moving an account because of its performance would let the firm cherry-pick composite results.

questions.concept: GIPS: composites, who may claim compliance, firm definition, requirements
questions.stem: Tavira Asset Management defines itself as the “firm” for GIPS purposes. At year-end it manages EUR 1,200m in discretionary, fee-paying portfolios and EUR 150m in a discretionary portfolio for its own staff pension plan, which pays no fee. It also manages EUR 90m in non-discretionary portfolios where the client must approve each trade before Tavira executes it. Separately, Tavira gives asset-allocation advice, without any trading authority, on EUR 400m of assets held by a consulting client. Total firm assets that Tavira should report in its compliant presentations are:

options.A: EUR 1,350m.
options.B: EUR 1,440m.
options.C: EUR 1,840m.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. EUR 1,350m is the discretionary assets only (1,200 + 150). It leaves out the non-discretionary assets that Tavira manages.

B is correct. Total firm assets include all discretionary and non-discretionary assets the firm manages, whether or not they pay a fee: 1,200 + 150 + 90 = EUR 1,440m. Advisory-only assets with no trading authority are assets under advisement and are not part of total firm assets (GIPS: firm definition and total firm assets).

C is incorrect. EUR 1,840m adds the EUR 400m of assets under advisement (1,440 + 400). Tavira has no trading authority over these assets, so they are not firm assets.

questions.concept: GIPS: composites, who may claim compliance, firm definition, requirements
questions.stem: Which of the following can claim compliance with the GIPS standards?

options.A: An individual portfolio manager who has met all of the requirements for the portfolios he or she manages.
options.B: A composite whose construction and return calculations meet all of the composite requirements.
options.C: An investment firm or asset owner that has met all of the applicable GIPS requirements.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Individual managers cannot claim GIPS compliance. Compliance is a firm-wide claim.

B is incorrect. Composites are presented by a compliant firm. A single composite, product or strategy cannot be claimed as “GIPS compliant” on its own.

C is correct. Only a firm (or an asset owner) can claim compliance, and it can do so only if it meets all applicable requirements. Compliance applies to the whole firm, not to parts of it.

questions.concept: Independence and objectivity I(B): gifts, issuer-paid research and travel
questions.stem: Anneke de Vries is a portfolio manager at Rhenish Investments and decides how the firm’s equity orders are allocated among approved brokers. One approved broker sends her two tickets to a sold-out international football final, worth about EUR 1,500, “as thanks for a great year together”. Rhenish has no written gift policy. De Vries’s best course of action is to:

options.A: accept the tickets and keep allocating orders strictly on best execution.
options.B: decline the tickets, because a gift of this size from a broker she allocates orders to could compromise her objectivity.
options.C: accept the tickets and disclose them to her supervisor in writing.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Her intention to stay objective is not enough. The Standard is concerned with what could reasonably be expected to compromise independence, and the appearance of a quid pro quo remains.

B is correct. Gifts that could reasonably be expected to affect a member’s independence and objectivity should be refused. A EUR 1,500 gift from a broker whose orders she controls creates that risk, and the best way to protect objectivity is to avoid the conflict (Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity).

C is incorrect. Disclosure is good practice and may be needed, but it does not remove the threat to objectivity. Disclosure is the minimum, not the best course of action.

questions.concept: Independence and objectivity I(B): gifts, issuer-paid research and travel
questions.stem: Anil Rao is a sell-side analyst who covers Kalvera Mining. Kalvera invites him on a site visit. Which of the following arrangements is least likely to compromise Rao’s independence and objectivity?

options.A: Rao accepts business-class flights and a five-star hotel from Kalvera for a plant that is easily reached by scheduled flights and ordinary hotels.
options.B: Rao accepts two additional days of personal holiday after the visit, paid for by Kalvera.
options.C: Rao flies on Kalvera’s private aircraft to a remote mine that has no scheduled air service, and his firm pays for his hotel and meals.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Lavish business-class flights and a five-star hotel are not needed for the visit. Commercial options exist, and the issuer-paid luxury would create a bias toward Kalvera.

B is incorrect. A holiday paid for by the issuer is a personal benefit unrelated to the work. It is the clearest threat to objectivity of the three.

C is correct. Analysts should normally pay their own transport and lodging, but where the only practical way to reach a remote site is the issuer’s aircraft, accepting that ride while the firm covers the other costs keeps Rao independent. This is the arrangement least likely to compromise him (Standard I(B)).

questions.concept: Suitability III(C): know the client, judge in portfolio context
questions.stem: Priya Nair advises Mr. Vasquez, 58, whose written IPS sets a moderate risk tolerance and a seven-year horizon to retirement. She recommends putting 5% of his portfolio into a volatile emerging-market small-cap fund. The remainder is diversified across global large-cap equities and investment-grade bonds, and her analysis shows that total portfolio risk stays within the limits of the IPS. Is the recommendation most likely consistent with her suitability duty?

options.A: Yes, because suitability is judged in the context of the total portfolio, and overall risk and return remain consistent with the client’s objectives and constraints.
options.B: Yes, but only after Mr. Vasquez signs a waiver acknowledging that the fund is riskier than his stated tolerance.
options.C: No, because a volatile small-cap fund is unsuitable for any client with a moderate risk tolerance.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Suitability is assessed for the portfolio as a whole, not investment by investment. A small allocation to a risky asset can be suitable if total portfolio risk and return stay within the client’s IPS (Standard III(C) Suitability).

B is incorrect. A waiver is not needed, and it would not make an unsuitable recommendation suitable. Here the total portfolio is within the IPS limits, so no waiver is required.

C is incorrect. This judges the fund in isolation. A risky asset can reduce or add little to total risk when held in a diversified portfolio.

questions.concept: Suitability III(C): know the client, judge in portfolio context
questions.stem: Tomas Bergström has managed Ms. Ilves’s portfolio for six years under an IPS that targets growth with high risk tolerance. Last month she told him that she has retired earlier than planned and will start drawing income from the portfolio within 12 months. Bergström has not changed the IPS. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?

options.A: Wait for the next scheduled annual review in eight months, because the Standards require updates only once a year.
options.B: Update the IPS now to reflect her changed circumstances, reassessing return objectives, risk tolerance and constraints, and review it again at least annually.
options.C: Keep the IPS in place, because the client has not formally asked him to change her objectives.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Annual reviews are a minimum, not a limit. A material change in circumstances triggers an update when it occurs.

B is correct. A member must make reasonable inquiry into a client’s situation and update it as circumstances change, as well as periodically (at least annually). Early retirement and an income need is a material change that calls for an immediate update (Standard III(C) Suitability).

C is incorrect. The duty to know the client is the adviser’s. He cannot wait for a formal request after learning of a material change.

questions.concept: Supervisors IV(C): inadequate compliance, suspected violation
questions.stem: Dagny Holm supervises the trading desk at Strand Capital. At lunch, a junior trader, Luis Ferrer, mentions that a friend at a listed company told him it will announce a takeover bid next week, and that he “bought a few shares in his own account this morning”. Holm is concerned that Ferrer may have traded on material nonpublic information. Her most appropriate immediate action is to:

options.A: wait until the bid is announced and the facts are confirmed before taking any action.
options.B: restrict Ferrer’s trading in the security, put the stock on the firm’s restricted list, and increase monitoring of his activity while compliance investigates.
options.C: warn Ferrer verbally not to trade on inside information and take no further action unless he does it again.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Delay would allow further trading and potentially further violations. The supervisor has to act when there are grounds for suspicion, not when the violation is proven.

B is correct. When a supervisor has reason to suspect a violation she must act promptly: restrict or monitor the employee’s activity and investigate, usually through compliance or legal, not just warn. (Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors).

C is incorrect. A verbal warning alone does not prevent further violations and does not start an investigation. The warning has to be backed by restriction and monitoring.

questions.concept: Supervisors IV(C): inadequate compliance, suspected violation
questions.stem: Karin Selwyn is offered the role of head of equities at Beacon Partners, a small advisory firm. During her due diligence she finds that Beacon has no written procedures for monitoring employees’ personal trading or for handling client complaints, and the owner says there is no budget to create them. Which course of action is most consistent with Selwyn’s supervisory responsibilities?

options.A: Decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until the firm adopts reasonable compliance procedures.
options.B: Accept the role and supervise her team informally using her own judgment, intending to press for written procedures later.
options.C: Accept the role and delegate compliance to the owner so that her own supervisory responsibility is limited.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A supervisor who finds that the firm’s compliance system is inadequate should decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until reasonable procedures are in place. She cannot supervise effectively without them (Standard IV(C)).

B is incorrect. Accepting the role without the procedures leaves her responsible for employees she cannot reasonably supervise. Good intentions do not replace the procedures.

C is incorrect. Delegation does not remove a supervisor’s responsibility for those under her supervision, and moving it to the owner who refuses to fund procedures does not solve the lack of a system.

questions.concept: Conflicts VI(A) and referral fees VI(C): what and when to disclose
questions.stem:
Samira Haddad is a portfolio manager at Keldon Asset Management. She is about to buy shares of Orvento plc for client portfolios. The following facts apply:

(1) Haddad personally owns shares in Orvento.
(2) Keldon’s affiliated investment bank is currently advising Orvento on a bond issue.
(3) Haddad will receive a fee from a trust company for introducing clients to it.
(4) Haddad receives a fixed annual salary from Keldon.

How many of these facts must be disclosed to clients under the Standards?

options.A: Two
options.B: Three
options.C: Four

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Two counts only the share ownership and the referral fee, and misses the firm-level investment banking relationship. Conflicts of the employer must be disclosed as well.

B is correct. Facts (1), (2) and (3) must be disclosed: personal ownership and the firm’s investment-banking relationship could impair independence (Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts), and the referral fee must be disclosed under VI(C) Referral Fees. Fact (4), an ordinary salary from her employer, is not a conflict, so the count is three.

C is incorrect. Four wrongly counts her regular salary. Standard compensation from the employer is expected by clients and is not a conflict of interest.

questions.concept: Conflicts VI(A) and referral fees VI(C): what and when to disclose
questions.stem: Elena Marchetti is an adviser at Calder Wealth. She agrees with a local law firm that it will pay her 15% of its first-year fees for each client she refers to it. She has not yet referred anyone. Under the Standards, Marchetti must disclose the arrangement to:

options.A: her clients only, once she has made her first referral and received the fee.
options.B: Calder Wealth, her clients and prospective clients, before they enter into an agreement for the law firm’s services.
options.C: Calder Wealth only, because the payment comes from a third party and not from clients.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Disclosure after the first referral and payment is too late. The disclosure has to come before the client agrees to the service.

B is correct. A member must disclose to the employer, clients and prospects any compensation or benefit received for recommending services, so that they can evaluate the possible bias in the recommendation. The disclosure must come before the client enters into any agreement for the services (Standard VI(C) Referral Fees).

C is incorrect. Disclosure to the employer alone leaves the clients without the information they need to judge the referral.

questions.concept: Diligence V(A) and communication V(B): research depth, fact vs forecast
questions.stem: Pieter Holm, an equity analyst at Brandt Securities, is told on Monday to initiate coverage of Nordhaven Shipping by Friday. He reads Nordhaven’s latest press release, takes consensus earnings estimates from a data vendor without examining how they were built, performs no valuation of his own, and publishes a “buy” with a price target. The report says clearly that the target is derived from vendor consensus numbers and the press release, and that it is Holm’s opinion. Holm has most likely:

options.A: not violated any Standard, because the report discloses its sources and labels the target as opinion.
options.B: violated only the requirement to distinguish fact from opinion and to disclose the limitations of his analysis.
options.C: violated the requirement for a reasonable and adequate basis for the recommendation, which disclosing the sources does not cure.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Disclosure of sources and labelling of opinion address communication, but they cannot make an unsupported recommendation acceptable.

B is incorrect. The report does separate fact and opinion and names its sources, so a communication violation is not what happened. The problem is the lack of analysis behind the recommendation.

C is correct. Holm had no reasonable and adequate basis: he did no analysis of his own and did not test the vendor numbers. That is a failure of diligence (Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis). Disclosing the sources is a communication matter and cannot supply the missing basis.

questions.concept: Diligence V(A) and communication V(B): research depth, fact vs forecast
questions.stem: Mei Lin Chow, a senior analyst at Aldgate Research, builds a detailed model of Corvette Motors’ earnings, tests its assumptions against industry data and concludes that the stock is attractive. Her published note says: “Corvette’s earnings will grow 18% a year for the next five years, so the stock will certainly double by 2031.” The note does not mention the model’s key assumptions or the risks. Chow’s note is most likely:

options.A: in violation, because she lacked a reasonable and adequate basis for her conclusion.
options.B: in violation, because it presents a forecast as a certainty and omits the assumptions and risks, even though her analytical basis was adequate.
options.C: consistent with the Standards, because her research was thorough and her analysis well supported.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. She did test her assumptions and had a model. The shortfall is in the wording and the omissions, not in her diligence.

B is correct. Chow’s analysis was sound, but the note presents a projection as a fact and does not disclose the assumptions and limitations. The communication to clients is the problem (Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients).

C is incorrect. A thorough basis does not cure a misleading presentation. The Standards also govern how the conclusions are communicated.

questions.concept: Performance presentation III(D): TWR vs MWR, composites in marketing
questions.stem: Nikolai Egorov manages a balanced fund sold through a retail platform. Investors decide when to deposit and withdraw, and Egorov has no control over these flows. The marketing brochure quotes the fund’s three-year return on a money-weighted basis, which is higher than the time-weighted return because investors added large sums shortly before a strong rally. Egorov’s firm should most appropriately present:

options.A: the change in net asset value per unit, ignoring distributions, to keep the figure simple.
options.B: the money-weighted return, because it reflects what investors actually earned.
options.C: the time-weighted return, because it removes the effect of cash flows that the manager does not control.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Ignoring distributions leaves out part of the total return, so the figure would not be complete as the Standard requires.

B is incorrect. The money-weighted return measures investors’ experience, which depends on the timing of their flows, not on the manager’s skill. It is inappropriate for assessing or marketing the manager’s performance.

C is correct. The manager cannot control external cash flows, so the time-weighted return is the fair and accurate measure of his investment performance. The money-weighted return here is flattered by investor timing, which would mislead prospective clients (Standard III(D) Performance Presentation).

questions.concept: Loyalty, prudence and care III(A): proxy voting, who is the client
questions.stem: Sven Aalto manages the defined-benefit pension plan of Brightwell Ltd. Brightwell’s finance director instructs him to route all of the plan’s equity trades through Hallmark Securities, which in return gives Brightwell’s treasury department a free market-data subscription. Aalto finds that Hallmark’s commissions are 6 basis points above comparable brokers and its execution quality is no better. Aalto’s best course of action is to:

options.A: decline to route the trades to Hallmark and select brokers on best execution for the benefit of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries.
options.B: follow the instruction, because Brightwell is the client that hired him and set his mandate.
options.C: follow the instruction and disclose the arrangement to the plan’s trustees.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Aalto’s duty runs to the plan participants and beneficiaries, not to the sponsor who hired him. Commissions are the plan’s assets, and soft-dollar benefits (such as research or data) may be accepted only if they benefit the clients who paid the commissions. Here the benefit goes to the sponsor and execution is worse, so he should use best execution (Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence and Care).

B is incorrect. The plan sponsor is not the beneficial client. Following the instruction would use plan assets to benefit the sponsor at the beneficiaries’ expense.

C is incorrect. Disclosure does not make it acceptable to pay higher commissions for no client benefit. The plan would still be bearing the cost of a benefit it does not receive.

questions.concept: Market manipulation II(B) and MNPI II(A)
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely an example of transaction-based market manipulation?

options.A: An analyst posts a false rumour on an investor forum that a small-cap company is under investigation, then buys the shares after the price falls.
options.B: A portfolio manager gives journalists false positive earnings estimates for a company that her clients hold.
options.C: A manager places a series of large buy orders in the final minutes of the last trading day of the quarter in an illiquid stock held by his clients, to lift the closing price.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Spreading a false rumour is information-based manipulation: the price is moved by misleading information, not by the trades.

B is incorrect. Leaking false earnings estimates is also information-based manipulation. No trading pattern is used to create a false price.

C is correct. Transaction-based manipulation uses trading itself to distort the price or the volume, such as marking the close in a thinly traded stock to inflate portfolio values (Standard II(B) Market Manipulation).

questions.concept: Market manipulation II(B) and MNPI II(A)
questions.stem: During a private call, the CFO of Torvald Engineering tells twelve invited analysts that its largest customer has cancelled a contract worth 30% of revenue. The company has not yet issued a press release or filing. Immediately after the call, Joon-ho Park, one of the analysts, sells his clients’ holdings of Torvald. Park has most likely:

options.A: violated the Standards, because he acted on material information that had not been disseminated to the public.
options.B: not violated the Standards, because twelve analysts heard the information, so it is already public.
options.C: not violated the Standards, because he traded for clients and not for his own account.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. The information was selectively disclosed to a small group and was not broadly disseminated, so it remains nonpublic. It is also material (30% of revenue), and trading on it breaches the prohibition on acting on material nonpublic information (Standard II(A)).

B is incorrect. Information is public only when it has been disseminated to the marketplace in general, not when a handful of analysts have heard it.

C is incorrect. The prohibition applies to trading for clients as well as for personal accounts. Trading for clients on MNPI is still a violation.

questions.concept: Misrepresentation I(C) and misconduct I(D)
questions.stem: Which of the following actions by a research analyst most likely violates the Standard on misrepresentation?

options.A: Citing a central bank’s published inflation series in a report and naming the source.
options.B: Using a vendor’s industry model after reviewing its assumptions and stating in the report that the model comes from the vendor.
options.C: Copying the forecasts, tables and conclusions from a competitor’s report into her own note without attribution and calling them “our estimates”.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Using publicly available data with an acknowledgement of the source is proper.

B is incorrect. Using third-party work is acceptable when its assumptions are checked and its source is acknowledged.

C is correct. Presenting someone else’s work as one’s own is plagiarism, a form of misrepresentation (Standard I(C) Misrepresentation).

questions.concept: Misrepresentation I(C) and misconduct I(D)
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a violation of the Standard on misconduct?

options.A: An analyst pays a parking fine incurred while driving to a client meeting.
options.B: An adviser submits an expense claim of EUR 640 for a client dinner that cost EUR 410, and keeps the difference.
options.C: A portfolio manager is dismissed by her employer after two years of weak performance.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. A minor parking fine does not involve dishonesty and does not reflect on professional integrity or competence.

B is correct. Falsifying an expense claim is dishonest and reflects adversely on the member’s integrity and professional reputation, which is misconduct (Standard I(D) Misconduct).

C is incorrect. Dismissal for poor performance is a competence or business matter, not dishonesty, fraud or deceit.

questions.concept: Fair dealing III(B) and priority of transactions VI(B)
questions.stem: Lars Nygaard, an analyst at Fjord Securities, downgrades Halbach Chemicals from “buy” to “sell”. Before the written report is published, he telephones the firm’s five largest institutional clients with the change and emails it to all other clients 40 minutes later. Fjord discloses to all clients that larger accounts receive more frequent reviews and personal calls. Nygaard’s action is most likely:

options.A: consistent with the Standards, because disclosed differences in service levels are permitted.
options.B: consistent with the Standards, because every client received the recommendation before the written report was published.
options.C: a violation, because some clients had a fair chance to act on the changed recommendation before others.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Different service levels (review frequency, calls) are acceptable, but the timing of a recommendation change is not a service level. Selective early notice is unfair.

B is incorrect. Receiving it before the report is published is not the test. The test is whether all clients had a fair opportunity to act at the same time.

C is correct. Clients may receive different levels of service if it is disclosed and does not disadvantage others, but a change in a recommendation must be disseminated so that all clients have a fair chance to act on it. Calling the largest clients first disadvantaged the rest (Standard III(B) Fair Dealing).

questions.concept: Fair dealing III(B) and priority of transactions VI(B)
questions.stem: Rashid Karim manages portfolios at Meridian Advisers. His mother holds a fee-paying managed account at Meridian that follows the same mandate as many of his other client accounts. An oversubscribed IPO is allocated to Karim’s portfolios. Which allocation approach is consistent with the Standards?

options.A: Allocate shares to her account on the same pro rata basis as to the other clients’ accounts.
options.B: Exclude his mother’s account, because family accounts may not take part in IPO allocations.
options.C: Fill her account only after all other clients’ accounts have been filled, to avoid any appearance of favouritism.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A family-member account that is a client account should be treated like any other client account, with no preferential or disadvantageous treatment (Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions and III(B) Fair Dealing).

B is incorrect. There is no rule that excludes family client accounts. Excluding her would treat her unfairly because of the relationship.

C is incorrect. Putting her at the back of the line disadvantages her account. Fair treatment means the same allocation rules as other clients.

questions.concept: Record retention V(C) and prior-employer work product
questions.stem: Hana Mizuno is leaving Sakura Securities to join a rival firm. Before leaving she copies to a USB drive the valuation models she built for Sakura, her research notes on the companies she covered, and Sakura’s client contact list, planning to use them in her new job. Asked about it, she says that she created the models herself and will keep the records for at least seven years, as recommended. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: The models, notes and client list were created during her employment and belong to Sakura, so she may not take or use them without its permission, although she may use general skills and public information at her new firm.
options.B: She may keep the models and notes, but not the client list, because only client information is confidential.
options.C: She may keep the models because she authored them, and seven years of retention satisfies the record-keeping Standard.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Work product created for an employer belongs to the employer. A former employee may take her skills, general knowledge and publicly available information but not the records, models or client lists. Record retention rules do not change who owns the records (Standard V(C) Record Retention and the duty to the former employer).

B is incorrect. The models and research notes are also the employer’s property. Confidentiality of client information is a separate issue.

C is incorrect. Authorship does not give ownership. Retention for seven years is the recommended minimum for the employer’s records, not a right to keep copies.

questions.concept: Loyalty to employer IV(A): whistleblowing, non-compete, independent practice
questions.stem: Oskar Lindh is a full-time analyst at Verde Capital. He wants to earn extra income by writing paid investment newsletters for retail subscribers at weekends, using his own computer and no firm information. Verde’s employment contract is silent on outside work. Which action is required before Lindh starts?

options.A: Obtain Verde’s written consent after describing the nature, compensation and time involved in the activity.
options.B: Nothing, because the work is done outside working hours and does not use firm resources.
options.C: Inform Verde within a month of starting, once he knows how the newsletter is doing.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Independent practice that may compete with the employer requires the employer’s written consent, given after the member discloses the nature, duration and compensation of the work (Standard IV(A) Loyalty).

B is incorrect. Working outside hours and avoiding firm resources do not remove the potential for competition. Written consent is still required.

C is incorrect. Telling the employer after the work has begun does not meet the requirement. Consent must come first.

questions.concept: Loyalty to employer IV(A): whistleblowing, non-compete, independent practice
questions.stem: Rafael Costa plans to leave Corvin Wealth and set up his own advisory firm. While he is still employed, which of the following actions is least likely to violate his duty of loyalty to Corvin?

options.A: Registering the new firm’s name with the authorities and renting office space in his own time, without using Corvin’s resources or approaching its clients.
options.B: Emailing Corvin’s clients during working hours to announce his departure and the launch of his new firm.
options.C: Copying the client contact list from Corvin’s CRM so that he can contact clients on the first day of his new firm.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A departing employee may make preparations to begin competing, such as registering a business and leasing space, provided he does so on his own time and does not use the employer’s resources or solicit its clients before he leaves (Standard IV(A)).

B is incorrect. Soliciting the employer’s clients during the employment, and on the employer’s time, is a violation.

C is incorrect. Taking client records is taking the employer’s property and prepares for solicitation, which breaches the duty of loyalty.

questions.concept: Ethics foundations: Code of Ethics, professionalism, ethical decision framework
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics?

options.A: Place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above their own personal interests.
options.B: Ensure that every client portfolio outperforms its benchmark in each measurement period.
options.C: Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. This is the first component of the Code of Ethics.

B is correct. The Code requires ethical conduct but does not promise outperformance. No member can guarantee that returns will beat a benchmark.

C is incorrect. This is a component of the Code of Ethics.

questions.concept: Ethics foundations: Code of Ethics, professionalism, ethical decision framework
questions.stem: Beatrix Lund, an analyst, is under pressure from her manager to publish a favourable note. She is working through the ethical decision-making framework: she is weighing the influence of that pressure on her judgment, checking the relevant laws, the Code and Standards and firm policy, and listing alternative courses of action. Which step of the framework is she most likely performing?

options.A: Identify
options.B: Decide and act
options.C: Consider

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Identify is about establishing the relevant facts, the stakeholders and duties owed, and any conflicts. Lund is already past that point.

B is incorrect. Decide and act comes after the alternatives have been evaluated. She is still comparing options.

C is correct. Weighing situational influences, applicable guidelines (laws, Code and Standards, firm policy) and alternative actions belongs to the Consider step of the framework (Identify, Consider, Decide and act, Reflect).

questions.concept: Confidentiality III(E) exceptions and Knowledge of law I(A)
questions.stem: Alvaro Beltran, an adviser, discovers during a review that his client Mr. Karlsen has been using his brokerage account to launder the proceeds of criminal activity. Which statement best describes Beltran’s position under the Standards?

options.A: He may disclose the information only after obtaining Mr. Karlsen’s written consent.
options.B: He may disclose the information to the proper authorities, because it concerns illegal activity by the client.
options.C: He must keep the information confidential, because the duty of confidentiality to a client is absolute.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Asking the client for consent is not needed for the exception to apply, and doing so could tip off a client who is committing a crime.

B is correct. Confidentiality is not absolute: a member may disclose information when it concerns illegal activity by the client, when disclosure is required by law, or when the client permits it (Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality).

C is incorrect. The duty has exceptions, including client illegal activity.

questions.concept: Confidentiality III(E) exceptions and Knowledge of law I(A)
questions.stem: Fiona Reilly, a CFA charterholder, works in a country where local securities law allows advisers to trade for their own accounts ahead of client orders if they report it to the regulator. Her firm has no policy on the subject. Reilly should:

options.A: follow the Code and Standards only for clients outside the country.
options.B: follow local law, because it is the governing standard in the jurisdiction in which she works.
options.C: follow the Code and Standards, which are stricter than local law, and not trade ahead of clients.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. There is no geographic carve-out. The Standards apply wherever the member works.

B is incorrect. The law sets a minimum, not the standard. When the Code is stricter, the Code applies.

C is correct. Members must comply with the stricter of applicable law and the Code and Standards. Where the Code is stricter than the law, Reilly must follow the Code and put clients ahead of her own account (Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law).

questions.concept: GIPS: verification, presentation and asset-owner basics
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about GIPS verification is least accurate?

options.A: A firm may choose to have verification carried out on a single composite rather than on the whole firm.
options.B: Verification is voluntary, but it must be performed by an independent third-party verifier.
options.C: Verification tests whether the firm has complied with the composite construction requirements on a firm-wide basis and whether its policies and procedures for calculating and presenting performance are designed to meet GIPS.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Verification is firm-wide. It cannot be performed on a single composite, and a firm cannot claim that one composite alone has been verified. This is the inaccurate statement.

B is incorrect. This is accurate: verification is optional and has to be done by an independent third party.

C is incorrect. This is accurate: it describes the two things a verifier tests.

questions.concept: CFA Program conduct VII(A)/(B): designation claims
questions.stem: Nia Okafor has passed the Level I and Level II CFA exams in consecutive years and is registered for Level III. Which of the following statements in her marketing materials is least likely to violate the Standards on referring to the CFA designation and program?

options.A: “Having passed both exams in consecutive years, Nia is a stronger investor than her peers.”
options.B: “Nia Okafor, CFA” on her business cards, because she has passed two of the three exams.
options.C: “Nia has passed Levels I and II of the CFA Program in consecutive years and is a candidate for Level III.”

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Passing the exams does not imply superior performance, and claiming that it does overstates the meaning of the program.

B is incorrect. Only a charterholder may use the CFA designation after her name. Passing exams does not entitle her to it.

C is correct. A factual statement of exams passed and her candidacy, without implying more, is permitted (Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation and the CFA Program).

questions.concept: Additional compensation IV(B) and responsibilities to employer
questions.stem: Marek Dvorak is a private banker at Alpen Trust. A long-standing client, delighted with performance, offers Dvorak a cash bonus of EUR 5,000 on top of Alpen’s regular fee. Alpen’s policies do not address bonuses paid by clients. Which action is required under the Standards?

options.A: Accept the bonus and tell Alpen at the next annual review.
options.B: Obtain written permission from Alpen before accepting the bonus.
options.C: Decline the bonus, because members may never accept additional compensation from clients.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Consent has to be obtained before accepting, not disclosed afterwards.

B is correct. Members must obtain written consent from their employer before accepting compensation or benefits from clients or third parties that could create a conflict with the employer’s interest (Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements). Declining is not required, only consent.

C is incorrect. Additional compensation is allowed with consent. Declining may be sensible but is not a requirement.

questions.concept: Hypothesis testing: Type I/II error, power, significance level wording
questions.stem: An analyst tests H0: the fund's mean monthly alpha is less than or equal to zero, against Ha: the fund's mean monthly alpha is greater than zero, at a 5% significance level. Which of the following statements about the test is least accurate?

options.A: Raising the significance level from 5% to 10%, all else equal, reduces the probability of a Type II error.
options.B: Increasing the sample size while keeping the significance level at 5% reduces the probability of a Type I error.
options.C: The power of the test is the probability of rejecting H<sub>0</sub> when the fund's true mean alpha is positive.

questions.explanation:
B is correct (the least accurate statement). The probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true H0) is the significance level the analyst chose, 5%. A bigger sample does not change it; it reduces the probability of a Type II error (and so raises power) because the standard error shrinks.

A is accurate, so it is not the answer. A higher significance level moves the critical value closer to zero, so H0 is rejected more easily: Type I probability rises, Type II probability falls (and power rises).

C is accurate, so it is not the answer. Power = 1 − P(Type II error) = P(reject H0 | H0 is false). H0 is false exactly when true alpha is positive. Rule: errors are always about H0: Type I = reject a true H0; Type II = fail to reject a false H0.

LOS: Type I and Type II errors, significance level and power of a test.

questions.concept: Test selection and calc: pooled t, paired t, chi-square single variance, F-test
questions.stem: An analyst compares the monthly returns of two equity funds, X and Y, over the same 36 months. The mean of the 36 monthly differences (X − Y) is 0.80% and the standard deviation of the differences is 2.40%. The sample standard deviations of the individual funds' returns are 4.00% (X) and 3.50% (Y). The analyst tests H0: μd = 0. The most appropriate test statistic is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. The two funds' returns are measured over the same months, so the samples are dependent and a paired-comparisons t-test on the differences is appropriate: t = (d̄ − μd0) / (sd/√n) = 0.80 / (2.40/√36) = 0.80 / 0.40 = 2.00, with 35 degrees of freedom.

B is incorrect. 0.90 comes from treating the samples as independent with a pooled variance: sp2 = (4.002 + 3.502)/2 = 14.125; SE = √(14.125 × (1/36 + 1/36)) = 0.886; t = 0.80/0.886 = 0.90. That ignores the pairing.

C is incorrect. 0.33 = 0.80/2.40 divides by the standard deviation of the differences instead of the standard error (forgot √n).

BA II Plus: 36 [2nd][√x] = 6; 2.4 [÷] 6 [=] 0.4; 0.8 [÷] 0.4 [=] 2.00.

LOS: choose the test for the situation (paired vs independent samples).

questions.concept: Regression: prediction interval (x t_c), SEE (n-2), un-log, forecast from equation
questions.stem:
A regression of a stock's monthly excess return (Y, in %) on the monthly change in a macroeconomic index (X, in index points) is estimated from 27 observations: Ŷ = 1.50 + 0.80X. The analyst wants a 95% prediction interval for Y when X = −3.0. The standard error of the forecast is 0.90. Critical t-values for 25 degrees of freedom: 1.708 (5% one-tail) and 2.060 (2.5% one-tail).

The 95% prediction interval for Y is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. Forecast: Ŷ = 1.50 + 0.80 × (−3.0) = −0.90%. Prediction interval = Ŷ ± tc × sf. A 95% two-sided interval with 27 − 2 = 25 degrees of freedom uses tc = 2.060: 2.060 × 0.90 = 1.854. Interval = −0.90 ± 1.854 = −2.75% to 0.95%.

A is incorrect. 2.05% to 5.75% drops the minus sign on X: 1.50 + 0.80 × 3 = 3.90, and 3.90 ± 1.854.

B is incorrect. −1.80% to 0.00% is −0.90 ± 0.90: the standard error of the forecast was used without multiplying by the critical t-value.

(Using 1.708, the one-tail value, would give −2.44% to 0.64%, which is a 90% interval, not 95%.)

BA II Plus: 0.8 [×] 3 [+/−] [+] 1.5 [=] −0.9; 2.06 [×] 0.9 [=] 1.854; −0.9 [−] 1.854 [=] −2.754; −0.9 [+] 1.854 [=] 0.954.

LOS: prediction intervals for the dependent variable.

questions.concept: Regression: prediction interval (x t_c), SEE (n-2), un-log, forecast from equation
questions.stem: An analyst estimates a log-linear model of a retailer's annual sales on real GDP growth: ln(Sales) = 1.20 + 0.35 × (GDP growth), where Sales is in £ millions and GDP growth is in percentage points. If GDP growth is forecast at −2.0%, the forecast sales are closest to:

options.A: £0.50 million
options.B: £1.65 million
options.C: £6.69 million

questions.explanation:
B is correct. ln(Sales) = 1.20 + 0.35 × (−2.0) = 0.50. The dependent variable is the natural log of sales, so un-log it: Sales = e0.50 = £1.65 million.

A is incorrect. £0.50 million is ln(Sales); the last step ex was skipped.

C is incorrect. £6.69 million = e1.90 comes from using GDP growth of +2.0% (sign of X lost): 1.20 + 0.70 = 1.90.

BA II Plus: 0.35 [×] 2 [+/−] [+] 1.2 [=] 0.5; [2nd][ex] 1.6487.

LOS: forecasting with a log-linear model; the dependent variable must be transformed back.

questions.concept: Regression: ANOVA F, R-squared vs r, slope t-test against non-zero H0, dummy interpretation
questions.stem:
A regression of a fund's monthly return on a single risk factor, estimated from a sample of 22 observations, produces the ANOVA table below. The estimated slope coefficient is negative.

SourcedfSum of squares
Regression1180
Residual20320
Total21500

The standard error of estimate and the sample correlation between the fund's return and the risk factor are closest to:

options.A: SEE = 4.00; correlation = −0.60
options.B: SEE = 3.81; correlation = −0.60
options.C: SEE = 4.00; correlation = −0.36

questions.explanation:
A is correct. SEE = √(SSE/(n − 2)) = √(320/20) = √16 = 4.00. R2 = SSR/SST = 180/500 = 0.36. In a one-variable regression r = ±√R2 = ±0.60, and the sign of r is the sign of the slope, so r = −0.60.

B is incorrect. SEE = 3.81 divides SSE by n = 22 instead of n − 2 = 20: √(320/22) = 3.81.

C is incorrect. −0.36 is R2 with a sign attached. R2 is the square of r, so r = −√0.36 = −0.60.

BA II Plus: 320 [÷] 20 [=] [√x] 4.00; 180 [÷] 500 [=] 0.36 [√x] 0.60, then [+/−].

LOS: ANOVA table, standard error of estimate, R2 and the correlation coefficient in simple regression.

questions.concept: Parametric vs nonparametric; Spearman rank correlation and correlation t-test
questions.stem: Which of the following situations is least likely to call for a nonparametric test?

options.A: An analyst has only the ordinal ranks that two rating agencies gave 30 funds and wants to test whether the two rankings are associated.
options.B: An analyst tests a claim about the median earnings change of a small sample of 12 firms that contains several extreme outliers.
options.C: An analyst tests whether the mean of 400 daily returns, drawn from an approximately normal population with unknown variance, differs from zero.

questions.explanation:
C is correct (least likely). Testing a mean from a large, approximately normal sample with unknown variance is the standard case for a parametric t-test. The distributional assumptions hold, so no substitute is needed.

A is incorrect. The data are ranks (ordinal), so a parametric test of Pearson correlation is not appropriate; the Spearman rank correlation test is the nonparametric tool.

B is incorrect. The sample is small, clearly non-normal and contains outliers, and the claim concerns a median, which is a parameter parametric tests do not address; a sign test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test fits.

Nonparametric tests are used when assumptions about the distribution are violated, data are ranks, or the hypothesis is not about a parameter.

LOS: situations in which nonparametric tests are appropriate.

questions.concept: Descriptive statistics: CV, sample vs population SD, harmonic/geometric mean, downside deviation
questions.stem: The annual returns on a fund over the last five years, treated as a sample, were 4%, 9%, 12%, 7% and 8%. The coefficient of variation of the returns is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. Mean = 8%. Squared deviations: 16, 1, 16, 1, 0, sum 34. Sample variance = 34/(5 − 1) = 8.5 (%2); sample standard deviation s = 2.9155%. CV = s / mean = 2.9155 / 8 = 0.36.

A is incorrect. 0.33 uses the population standard deviation (divides by n = 5): √6.8 = 2.608; 2.608/8 = 0.33. The returns are a sample, so divide by n − 1.

C is incorrect. 2.74 is mean/standard deviation (8/2.9155), the inverse of the CV.

BA II Plus: [2nd][DATA], enter 4 [ENTER][↓] 9 [ENTER][↓] … 8 [ENTER]; [2nd][STAT] until 1-V; [↓] to read x̄ = 8 and Sx = 2.9155 (use Sx, not σx). 2.9155 [÷] 8 [=] 0.3644.

LOS: coefficient of variation; sample vs population standard deviation.

questions.concept: Covariance, correlation and expected value/variance from probability tables
questions.stem:
An analyst models the one-year returns on two assets, A and B, under three economic scenarios:

ScenarioProbabilityReturn on AReturn on B
Strong0.3012%8%
Normal0.506%4%
Weak0.20−4%0%

The covariance between the returns on A and B is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. E(RA) = 0.3(12) + 0.5(6) + 0.2(−4) = 5.8%; E(RB) = 0.3(8) + 0.5(4) + 0.2(0) = 4.4%. Cov = Σ Pi (RA,i − 5.8)(RB,i − 4.4) = 0.3(6.2)(3.6) + 0.5(0.2)(−0.4) + 0.2(−9.8)(−4.4) = 6.696 − 0.04 + 8.624 = 15.28 (%2).

B is incorrect. 21.79 is the simple average of the three cross-products (65.36/3), ignoring the scenario probabilities.

C is incorrect. 40.80 is E(RARB) = 0.3(96) + 0.5(24) + 0.2(0). Covariance = E(RARB) − E(RA)E(RB) = 40.80 − 25.52 = 15.28; the expected-return product was not subtracted.

BA II Plus: 0.3 [×] 6.2 [×] 3.6 [=] 6.696; add 0.5 [×] 0.2 [×] 0.4 [+/−] [=] −0.04 and 0.2 [×] 9.8 [×] 4.4 [=] 8.624 (the two negatives multiply to a positive).

LOS: expected value and covariance from a joint probability table.

questions.concept: Time value of money: annuities, EAR, loan amortisation
questions.stem: A borrower takes a £300,000 mortgage with a 25-year term and a stated annual rate of 4.5% compounded monthly. Level payments are made at the end of each month. The monthly payment is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. Monthly rate = 4.5%/12 = 0.375%; N = 25 × 12 = 300. PMT = 300,000 × 0.00375 / (1 − 1.00375−300) = £1,667.50.

A is incorrect. £1,661.27 is the payment with the calculator left in BGN (annuity-due) mode: 1,667.50 / 1.00375. Payments here are at the end of each month.

B is incorrect. £1,685.98 treats the loan as annual-pay (N = 25, I/Y = 4.5): payment £20,231.71, divided by 12. That ignores monthly compounding within the year.

BA II Plus: [2nd][BGN] check it shows END ([2nd][SET] if needed); [2nd][CLR TVM]; 300 [N]; 0.375 [I/Y]; 300000 [PV]; 0 [FV]; [CPT][PMT] = −1,667.50.

LOS: loan amortisation; ordinary annuity payment.

questions.concept: Probability: Bayes, total probability, counting rules, probability trees
questions.stem: A bank's credit model labels each borrower as "flagged" or "not flagged". Historically 20% of borrowers default within a year. The model flags 85% of the borrowers who go on to default and 10% of those who do not. A borrower is flagged. The probability that this borrower defaults within a year is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Bayes' formula: P(default | flag) = P(flag | default) P(default) / P(flag). P(flag) = 0.85 × 0.20 + 0.10 × 0.80 = 0.17 + 0.08 = 0.25. So P(default | flag) = 0.17 / 0.25 = 0.68.

B is incorrect. 0.85 is P(flag | default), the model's hit rate; it reverses the conditioning.

C is incorrect. 0.17 is the joint probability P(flag and default) = 0.85 × 0.20; the division by P(flag) was skipped.

BA II Plus: 0.85 [×] 0.2 [=] 0.17 [STO]1; 0.1 [×] 0.8 [=] 0.08 [+] [RCL]1 [=] 0.25; 0.17 [÷] 0.25 [=] 0.68.

LOS: Bayes' formula, total probability.

questions.concept: Confidence intervals, standard error, t vs z, degrees of freedom
questions.stem: An analyst draws a random sample of 25 monthly returns from a population assumed to be normally distributed with unknown variance. The sample mean is 1.2% and the sample standard deviation is 3.0%. Relevant critical values: t0.025,24 = 2.064 and z0.025 = 1.96. The 95% confidence interval for the population mean is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. Population variance unknown and population normal: use the t-distribution with n − 1 = 24 degrees of freedom. SE = s/√n = 3.0/5 = 0.60. Interval = 1.2 ± 2.064 × 0.60 = 1.2 ± 1.238 = −0.04% to 2.44%.

A is incorrect. 0.02% to 2.38% uses z = 1.96 (1.2 ± 1.176). With an unknown variance and n = 25, the t-value is required; the interval is too narrow and wrongly excludes zero.

B is incorrect. −4.99% to 7.39% multiplies t by the standard deviation (3.0) instead of the standard error (0.60), i.e. forgot to divide by √n.

BA II Plus: 3 [÷] 25 [√x] [=] 0.6; [×] 2.064 [=] 1.2384; 1.2 [−] 1.2384 [=] −0.0384; 1.2 [+] 1.2384 [=] 2.4384.

LOS: confidence intervals; t vs z; standard error of the sample mean.

questions.concept: Simulation and lognormal; Big Data and ML terminology
questions.stem: A data scientist trains a supervised model on 5,000 labelled observations to classify companies as likely or unlikely to restate earnings. The model classifies 98% of the training sample correctly but only 72% of a separate validation sample. The best description of the problem and the most appropriate response is:

options.A: underfitting; add more features and increase the model's complexity.
options.B: overfitting; reduce model complexity (for example by regularization) and use k-fold cross-validation.
options.C: no problem; a gap of this size between training and validation accuracy is normal and no action is needed.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. High accuracy in-sample and much lower accuracy out-of-sample is the signature of overfitting: the model has learned noise specific to the training data. Remedies are a simpler model or regularization/penalties, more training data, and k-fold cross-validation to tune complexity.

A is incorrect. Underfitting means poor performance on both training and validation data. Making the model more complex would worsen overfitting.

C is incorrect. A small gap is expected, but a 26-point drop signals poor generalisation, so action is needed.

LOS: overfitting, underfitting and cross-validation in machine learning.

questions.concept: FX calculations: cross rates, forward points, triangular arbitrage, appreciation vs depreciation
questions.stem: A dealer quotes USD/GBP = 1.2800 and USD/EUR = 1.0800, both in price currency/base currency terms (USD per one GBP and USD per one EUR). The implied EUR/GBP cross rate, in euros per one pound, is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. 1 GBP = 1.2800 USD and 1 EUR = 1.0800 USD, so 1 GBP = 1.2800 / 1.0800 = 1.1852 EUR. EUR/GBP = (USD/GBP) / (USD/EUR) = 1.1852. The USD cancels.

B is incorrect. 0.8438 = 1.0800 / 1.2800 is the inverse (GBP/EUR, pounds per euro).

C is incorrect. 1.3824 = 1.2800 × 1.0800 multiplies the two quotes; dollars would not cancel.

BA II Plus: 1.28 [÷] 1.08 [=] 1.1852.

LOS: cross-rate calculation.

questions.concept: FX calculations: cross rates, forward points, triangular arbitrage, appreciation vs depreciation
questions.stem: The USD/EUR exchange rate (USD per one EUR) rises from 1.0800 to 1.1016. Relative to the euro, the US dollar has most likely:

options.A: depreciated by 2.00%.
options.B: depreciated by 1.96%.
options.C: appreciated by 2.00%.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. A rise in USD/EUR means the euro (base currency) appreciated: 1.1016/1.0800 − 1 = +2.00%. The dollar is the price currency. In euros per dollar, the rate fell from 1/1.0800 = 0.9259 to 1/1.1016 = 0.9078, a change of 1.0800/1.1016 − 1 = −1.96%. The dollar depreciated by 1.96%.

A is incorrect. The 2.00% is the euro's appreciation (the base currency's percentage change); the dollar's depreciation must be measured on the inverted quote, giving 1.96%.

C is incorrect. The size is the euro's move and the direction is wrong: a higher USD price of the euro means the dollar buys fewer euros, so it weakened.

BA II Plus: 1.08 [÷] 1.1016 [=] 0.9804; [−] 1 [=] −0.0196.

LOS: percentage appreciation/depreciation of base and price currencies.

questions.concept: Exchange-rate regimes and trade-balance effects (absorption, Marshall-Lerner)
questions.stem: A country runs a trade deficit and its economy is operating at full employment. Its currency depreciates. According to the absorption approach, the trade balance will most likely improve only if:

options.A: the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds one.
options.B: domestic absorption rises faster than national income.
options.C: domestic absorption (spending) falls relative to national income.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. Trade balance = national income (output) − domestic absorption. At full employment, depreciation cannot raise output, so the deficit shrinks only if domestic spending falls relative to income (or capacity allows income to rise).

A is incorrect. This is the Marshall-Lerner condition of the elasticities approach, not the absorption approach.

B is incorrect. Absorption rising faster than income would widen the deficit.

LOS: effect of exchange-rate changes on the trade balance: elasticities and absorption approaches.

questions.concept: Fiscal policy: multiplier, crowding out, automatic stabilisers
questions.stem: In an economy the marginal propensity to consume out of disposable income is 0.75 and the income tax rate is 20%. The government increases spending by €40 billion, financed by borrowing, with no change in tax rates and no crowding out of private spending. The increase in real GDP is closest to:

options.A: €100 billion
options.B: €160 billion
options.C: €47 billion

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Fiscal multiplier = 1 / [1 − MPC(1 − t)] = 1 / [1 − 0.75 × 0.80] = 1 / 0.40 = 2.5. ΔGDP = 2.5 × 40 = €100 billion.

B is incorrect. €160 billion uses the multiplier without taxes, 1/(1 − MPC) = 4.

C is incorrect. €47 billion uses 1 / (1 − MPC × t) = 1/0.85, applying the tax rate where (1 − t) belongs.

BA II Plus: 0.75 [×] 0.8 [=] 0.6; 1 [−] 0.6 [=] 0.4; [1/x] 2.5; [×] 40 [=] 100.

LOS: fiscal multiplier.

questions.concept: Monetary policy: tools, neutral rate, central bank roles and independence
questions.stem: A central bank targets inflation of 2.0% and estimates the real trend rate of economic growth at 1.5%. The current policy rate is 3.0%. The central bank's policy stance is best described as:

options.A: contractionary, because the policy rate exceeds the 2.0% inflation target.
options.B: expansionary, because the policy rate is below the neutral rate.
options.C: contractionary, because the real policy rate is positive.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Neutral nominal policy rate = real trend growth + target inflation = 1.5% + 2.0% = 3.5%. The policy rate of 3.0% is below it, so policy is expansionary (stimulative).

A is incorrect. The comparison is with the neutral rate (3.5%), not with the inflation target alone.

C is incorrect. The real policy rate is 3.0% − 2.0% = +1.0%, but the benchmark is the real neutral rate (the 1.5% trend growth rate). 1.0% < 1.5%, so policy is still expansionary.

LOS: the neutral interest rate and the stance of monetary policy.

questions.concept: Business cycle phases and indicators
questions.stem: An economy shows these conditions: real GDP growth is positive but decelerating; unemployment is at a multi-year low; wage and price inflation are accelerating; the central bank is raising its policy rate; and the inventory-to-sales ratio is rising. The economy is most likely in:

options.A: an early expansion.
options.B: a recession.
options.C: a late expansion.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. Late expansion: growth positive but slowing, tight labor markets, accelerating wages and inflation, tightening monetary policy, and inventories building as sales soften.

A is incorrect. In an early expansion, unemployment is high but falling, inflation is low and often falling, and policy is accommodative.

B is incorrect. A recession features falling real GDP and rising unemployment, not an unemployment low and positive growth.

LOS: phases of the business cycle and typical indicators.

questions.concept: Market structures: HHI, Nash equilibrium, long-run competition
questions.stem: In an industry, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is computed with market shares expressed in percent. Two firms with market shares of 15% and 12% propose to merge, and the combined firm is expected to hold a 27% share. The increase in the HHI caused by the merger is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. Before: 152 + 122 = 225 + 144 = 369. After: 272 = 729. Increase = 729 − 369 = 360 = 2 × 15 × 12.

A is incorrect. 180 = 15 × 12 omits the factor 2 from (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2.

C is incorrect. 369 is the sum of the two firms' squared shares before the merger, not the change.

BA II Plus: 2 [×] 15 [×] 12 [=] 360.

LOS: HHI and the effect of mergers on concentration.

questions.concept: Geopolitics, globalisation, trading blocs
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about trading blocs is least accurate?

options.A: A common market requires its members to adopt a single currency.
options.B: A customs union adopts a common set of tariffs on imports from non-member countries.
options.C: In a free trade area, members remove barriers to trade among themselves but each sets its own tariffs on non-members.

questions.explanation:
A is correct (least accurate). A common market allows free movement of goods, services and factors of production (labor and capital) among members. A single currency is a feature of a monetary union, the step beyond an economic union.

B is accurate. This defines a customs union: free internal trade plus a common external tariff.

C is accurate. In a free trade area, there is no common external tariff, each member keeps its own.

Ladder: free trade area, customs union, common market, economic union, monetary union.

LOS: forms of regional integration.

questions.concept: Comparative advantage, tariffs, quotas, trade restrictions
questions.stem: Country M imports steel. Its government compares a tariff with an import quota that limits imports to the same quantity as the tariff would, all else equal. The quota licences are given free to foreign exporters. Compared with the tariff, the quota will most likely result in:

options.A: a smaller rise in the domestic price of steel.
options.B: higher government revenue.
options.C: quota rents accruing to foreign exporters rather than tariff revenue going to Country M's government.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. With the same import quantity, the domestic price is the same. The gap between domestic and world price is a tariff revenue under a tariff, but under a quota with licences allocated to foreign exporters it becomes quota rent captured by them. Country M's welfare loss is therefore larger.

A is incorrect. The same import quantity implies the same domestic price, consumer surplus loss and domestic production gain.

B is incorrect. The tariff raises government revenue; a quota with free licences raises none.

LOS: effects of tariffs and quotas on welfare.

questions.concept: Elasticity, breakeven and shutdown points, monopoly and monopolistic competition
questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm faces a market price of £8.00 per unit. At its current output, average total cost is £9.50 and average variable cost is £7.20. In the short run, the firm should most appropriately:

options.A: shut down immediately, because price is below average total cost.
options.B: continue to operate, because price exceeds average variable cost, and exit in the long run if price stays below average total cost.
options.C: continue to operate in both the short and the long run, because price exceeds average variable cost.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Price (8.00) exceeds AVC (7.20), so each unit contributes £0.80 towards fixed costs; operating loses £1.50 per unit but shutting down would lose all fixed costs. In the long run all costs are variable, so the firm exits if price stays below ATC.

A is incorrect. The short-run shutdown test compares price with AVC, not ATC.

C is incorrect. Covering AVC justifies short-run operation only; a long-run loss (P < ATC) leads to exit.

LOS: breakeven and shutdown points under perfect competition.

questions.concept: Balance of payments and capital flows
questions.stem: Which of the following changes would be least likely to widen a country's current account deficit?

options.A: An increase in private-sector saving, with investment and the government budget balance unchanged.
options.B: An increase in the government budget deficit, with private saving and investment unchanged.
options.C: A surge in domestic business investment, with private saving and the government budget balance unchanged.

questions.explanation:
A is correct (least likely). Current account = (Sprivate − I) + (T − G). Higher private saving raises (S − I) and narrows the deficit (less need to borrow from abroad).

B is incorrect (it widens the deficit). A larger budget deficit lowers (T − G).

C is incorrect (it widens the deficit). Higher investment lowers (S − I), so more capital must be imported.

LOS: balance of payments, saving–investment identity.

questions.concept: Deferred taxes: DTA vs DTL (incl. liabilities), difference x rate, tax expense sign rule
questions.stem: Brandt AG's tax note shows income tax payable of €520 million for the year. Over the year its deferred tax liability decreased from €150 million to €110 million, and its deferred tax asset increased from €30 million to €45 million. Income tax expense in the income statement is closest to:

options.A: €465 million
options.B: €495 million
options.C: €545 million

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA = 520 + (−40) − (+15) = €465 million. A falling DTL means that, on balance, more tax is being paid than expensed, so expense is below the amount payable; a rising DTA means tax has been prepaid, which also lowers expense.

B is incorrect. This is 520 − 40 + 15: the DTL change has the right sign but the rise in the DTA was added instead of subtracted. A higher DTA reduces tax expense relative to taxes payable.

C is incorrect. This is 520 + 40 − 15: the fall in the DTL was treated as a rise (+40). A DTL that falls must be subtracted from taxes payable.

BA II Plus: No special worksheet. Key: 520 − 40 − 15 = 465 (enter the DTL change as −40 and the DTA change as +15, then subtract the DTA change).

questions.concept: Deferred taxes: DTA vs DTL (incl. liabilities), difference x rate, tax expense sign rule
questions.stem: Larkin Corp. (enacted tax rate 30%) recognises a €240,000 provision for product warranties in its first year of operation. For tax purposes, warranty costs are deductible only when claims are paid, and no claims were paid during the year. At year-end Larkin will most likely report:

options.A: a deferred tax liability of €72,000.
options.B: no deferred tax, because the difference is permanent.
options.C: a deferred tax asset of €72,000.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. This reverses the direction. The DTA/DTL rule is flipped for liabilities: carrying amount above tax base is a DTL for an asset but a DTA for a liability.

B is incorrect. A permanent difference never reverses (for example, a fine that is never deductible). The warranty expense will become deductible when claims are paid, so this is a temporary difference.

C is correct. The warranty liability has a carrying amount of €240,000 and a tax base of zero (the carrying amount less the amount deductible in future periods is 240,000 − 240,000 = 0). A liability whose carrying amount exceeds its tax base creates a deductible temporary difference: Larkin expenses the cost for reporting now but deducts it for tax later, so it pays more tax today. DTA = 240,000 × 30% = €72,000.

BA II Plus: 240,000 × 0.30 = 72,000.

questions.concept: Deferred taxes: DTA vs DTL (incl. liabilities), difference x rate, tax expense sign rule
questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely to result in a deferred tax liability?

options.A: Using accelerated depreciation for financial reporting and straight-line depreciation for tax.
options.B: Using accelerated depreciation for tax and straight-line depreciation for financial reporting.
options.C: Recognising revenue on a long-term contract for financial reporting before it is taxable.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Accelerated depreciation for reporting gives a lower carrying amount than the tax base. Taxable income is higher than pretax income now, so the company pays more tax today and has a deferred tax asset, not a liability. The rule: whoever deducts the expense first has the lower taxes today and the DTL.

B is incorrect. Tax depreciation is higher in the early years, so taxable income is lower than pretax income and tax is deferred. Carrying amount exceeds tax base, which creates a DTL.

C is incorrect. Revenue is recorded now but taxed later, so taxable income is lower than pretax income today. The tax is deferred and a DTL is created.

questions.concept: Diluted EPS: convertible bonds/preferred, options (TSM), antidilution
questions.stem:
Marlowe Inc. reported net income of $1,500,000 and had 500,000 common shares outstanding throughout the year. It also had:

  • non-convertible preferred stock with annual dividends of $100,000;
  • convertible preferred stock with annual dividends of $120,000, convertible into 100,000 common shares;
  • options to buy 60,000 common shares at $20, with an average market price of $30 during the year.

Diluted EPS is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. $2.06 = (1,500,000 − 100,000 − 120,000) / 620,000. The numerator still deducts the convertible preferred dividend even though the shares are added: the dividend must be added back when conversion is assumed.

B is incorrect. $2.12 = 1,400,000 / (500,000 + 100,000 + 60,000). All 60,000 option shares were added instead of the treasury stock method net of 20,000 shares repurchased with the exercise proceeds.

C is correct. Basic EPS = (1,500,000 − 100,000 − 120,000) / 500,000 = $2.56. The convertible preferred is dilutive (120,000 / 100,000 = $1.20 per incremental share is below $2.56), so its dividend is added back but the non-convertible dividend still comes off. Treasury stock method: 60,000 − (60,000 × 20 / 30) = 20,000 net new shares. Diluted EPS = (1,500,000 − 100,000) / (500,000 + 100,000 + 20,000) = 1,400,000 / 620,000 = $2.26.

BA II Plus: Numerator: 1,500,000 − 100,000 = 1,400,000. Shares: 60,000 × (1 − 20 ÷ 30) = 20,000 (keys: 1 − 20 ÷ 30 = 0.3333, × 60,000 = 20,000). Then 1,400,000 ÷ 620,000 = 2.258.

questions.concept: Diluted EPS: convertible bonds/preferred, options (TSM), antidilution
questions.stem:
Vantor Ltd. reported net income of £800,000 and a weighted average of 400,000 shares, so basic EPS is £2.00. The tax rate is 25%. Potentially dilutive securities outstanding all year:

  • 6% convertible bonds: annual interest expense of £120,000 (before tax), convertible into 25,000 shares;
  • options on 40,000 shares at an exercise price of £15, with an average market price of £25.

Diluted EPS is closest to:

options.A: £1.92
options.B: £2.00
options.C: £2.02

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Options: 40,000 − (40,000 × 15 / 25) = 16,000 incremental shares, which lowers EPS to 800,000 / 416,000 = £1.923. The bonds add 120,000 × (1 − 0.25) = 90,000 of income for 25,000 shares, or £3.60 per incremental share, which exceeds EPS of £1.92 (and basic EPS of £2.00). They are antidilutive and are excluded. Diluted EPS = £1.92.

B is incorrect. Diluted EPS equal to basic would require that no security be dilutive. The options are dilutive because their exercise price is below the average market price.

C is incorrect. £2.02 = (800,000 + 90,000) / (400,000 + 16,000 + 25,000). Including the bonds raises EPS above the figure without them, which signals antidilution. Diluted EPS can never be higher than basic EPS.

BA II Plus: 800,000 ÷ 416,000 = 1.923. Antidilution check: 90,000 ÷ 25,000 = 3.60 > 1.92.

questions.concept: FCFF and FCFE from NI/CFO (payables sign, Int(1-t), net borrowing)
questions.stem: A company reports the following for the year (in £ millions): net income 240; depreciation 80; interest expense 50; tax rate 30%; capital expenditures 150; accounts receivable increased by 40; accounts payable increased by 30. Free cash flow to the firm is closest to:

options.A: £135 million
options.B: £195 million
options.C: £210 million

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. £135 million subtracts the rise in payables (WCInv = 40 + 30 = 70). Liability increases must be added.

B is correct. FCFF = NI + non-cash charges + Int(1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv. Int(1 − t) = 50 × 0.70 = 35. Working capital investment = ΔAR − ΔAP = 40 − 30 = 10 (a rise in a liability is a source of cash). FCFF = 240 + 80 + 35 − 150 − 10 = £195 million.

C is incorrect. £210 million adds back the full interest of 50 rather than after-tax interest of 35.

BA II Plus: 50 × 0.7 = 35; 240 + 80 + 35 − 150 − 40 + 30 = 195.

questions.concept: FCFF and FCFE from NI/CFO (payables sign, Int(1-t), net borrowing)
questions.stem: A Swiss manufacturer reports (in CHF millions): net income 300; depreciation 90; inventory increased by 40; accounts payable decreased by 25; capital expenditures 180; new borrowing 100; debt repayment 160. Free cash flow to equity is closest to:

options.A: CHF 85 million
options.B: CHF 135 million
options.C: CHF 205 million

questions.explanation:
A is correct. FCFE = NI + NCC − FCInv − WCInv + net borrowing. WCInv = 40 (inventory up) + 25 (payables down, a use of cash) = 65. Net borrowing = 100 − 160 = −60. FCFE = 300 + 90 − 180 − 65 − 60 = CHF 85 million.

B is incorrect. CHF 135 million treats the fall in payables as a source of cash (+25): 300 + 90 − 40 + 25 − 180 − 60. A decrease in a liability is an outflow.

C is incorrect. CHF 205 million adds the repayment as if it were positive net borrowing (+60). The company repaid more than it borrowed, so net borrowing is negative.

BA II Plus: 300 + 90 − 40 − 25 − 180 + 100 − 160 = 85.

questions.concept: Long-lived assets: capitalised interest, impairment, revaluation, depreciation effects on ratios
questions.stem: Orvale Corp., a US GAAP reporter, borrows to build its own production plant and capitalises the related interest rather than expensing it. Compared with expensing the interest, capitalising it will most likely result, in the year of capitalisation, in:

options.A: a lower interest coverage ratio and a higher cash flow from operations.
options.B: a higher interest coverage ratio and a higher cash flow from operations.
options.C: a higher interest coverage ratio and an unchanged cash flow from operations.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. CFO is higher, but interest coverage is higher too, not lower: the reported interest expense in the denominator is smaller. (Analysts often add capitalised interest back to the denominator to adjust, but the reported ratio rises.)

B is correct. Capitalised interest is added to the asset instead of being expensed, so reported interest expense is lower and net income and EBIT-based interest coverage (EBIT / interest expense) are higher in the year. Under US GAAP the cash paid for capitalised interest is an investing outflow (part of the cost of the plant), whereas expensed interest is an operating outflow, so CFO is higher and CFI is lower. Depreciation of the larger asset depresses income in later years.

C is incorrect. Coverage is higher, but CFO is not unchanged. Capitalised interest is reclassified from operating to investing cash flow under US GAAP, so CFO increases.

questions.concept: Long-lived assets: capitalised interest, impairment, revaluation, depreciation effects on ratios
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about impairment of long-lived assets held for use is least accurate?

options.A: Under IFRS, an impairment loss may be reversed, but only up to the carrying amount that would have existed had no impairment been recognised.
options.B: Under US GAAP, an impairment loss is recognised only if the asset's carrying amount exceeds the undiscounted expected future cash flows.
options.C: Under US GAAP, an impairment loss is reversed if the asset's fair value later recovers.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Accurate. IFRS allows reversal when the recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use) rises, capped at depreciated historical cost. Goodwill impairments are never reversed.

B is incorrect. Accurate. US GAAP is a two-step test: the asset is impaired if carrying amount exceeds the sum of undiscounted future cash flows, and the loss is then measured as carrying amount less fair value. IFRS has a one-step test using the recoverable amount.

C is correct. US GAAP prohibits reversal of impairment losses on assets held for use. After impairment the written-down amount becomes the new cost basis. This is the false statement.

questions.concept: Inventory: LIFO vs FIFO vs weighted average, LIFO liquidation, LCNRV US GAAP vs IFRS
questions.stem: In a period of rising prices, a LIFO company sells more units than it purchases, so layers of older, lower-cost inventory are liquidated. Compared with a year without liquidation, this will most likely result in:

options.A: lower cost of goods sold and higher income taxes paid.
options.B: higher cost of goods sold and lower income taxes paid.
options.C: lower cost of goods sold and lower income taxes paid.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Liquidating old, low-cost layers charges them to COGS instead of current-cost purchases, so COGS is lower and gross profit is inflated. Higher taxable income means higher income taxes paid, which is a cash cost of the "paper" profit.

B is incorrect. This is the effect of LIFO in rising prices when no liquidation occurs (COGS at current cost), not of liquidation.

C is incorrect. COGS is lower, but lower COGS raises taxable income, so taxes paid rise rather than fall.

questions.concept: Inventory: LIFO vs FIFO vs weighted average, LIFO liquidation, LCNRV US GAAP vs IFRS
questions.stem: At the end of Year 1, inventory with a cost of 500,000 (FIFO) is written down to its net realisable value (NRV) of 420,000. At the end of Year 2 the same inventory is still on hand and its NRV has risen to 560,000. Assuming one company reports under IFRS and an identical company under US GAAP, the Year 2 carrying amounts are:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. IFRS allows reversal of an inventory write-down when NRV recovers, limited to the original cost: the carrying amount returns to 500,000 (the lower of cost 500,000 and NRV 560,000). US GAAP does not allow reversal of a write-down for FIFO or average-cost inventory; the written-down 420,000 becomes the new cost basis.
