B is incorrect. Inventory can never be carried above original cost under either framework. IFRS caps the reversal at 500,000 and US GAAP prohibits it altogether.

C is incorrect. The frameworks are reversed. It is IFRS that permits reversal (up to original cost); US GAAP does not.

questions.concept: Revenue recognition: percentage of completion, bill-and-hold, contract steps
questions.stem: A contractor signs a fixed-price contract to build a facility for £8,000,000 with revenue recognised over time using costs incurred as a share of total expected costs. Original total cost estimate: £6,000,000. In Year 1 costs incurred were £1,800,000. In Year 2 costs incurred were £2,700,000 and the estimate of total contract costs was revised to £6,400,000. Revenue recognised in Year 2 is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Year 1: 1.8 / 6.0 = 30%, revenue 2,400,000. At the end of Year 2 cumulative costs are 4,500,000, so progress = 4,500,000 / 6,400,000 = 70.3125% and cumulative revenue = 5,625,000. Year 2 revenue = 5,625,000 − 2,400,000 = £3,225,000.

B is incorrect. £3,600,000 keeps the original estimate: 4,500,000 / 6,000,000 = 75%, cumulative 6,000,000, less 2,400,000. The revised cost estimate must be used.

C is incorrect. £5,625,000 is the cumulative revenue at the end of Year 2. The 2,400,000 recognised in Year 1 has not been deducted.

BA II Plus: 4,500,000 ÷ 6,400,000 = 0.703125; × 8,000,000 = 5,625,000; − 2,400,000 = 3,225,000.

questions.concept: DuPont, ROE vs required return, sustainable growth
questions.stem: A company has a tax rate of 30%, interest expense equal to 20% of EBIT, an EBIT margin of 15%, total asset turnover of 1.2 and a financial leverage ratio (assets / equity) of 2.0. It pays out 40% of net income as dividends. Using the five-component DuPont decomposition, the sustainable growth rate is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. 8.1% multiplies ROE by the payout ratio (0.40) instead of the retention ratio (0.60).

B is correct. ROE = tax burden × interest burden × EBIT margin × turnover × leverage = 0.70 × 0.80 × 0.15 × 1.2 × 2.0 = 20.16%. Sustainable growth = ROE × retention = 20.16% × (1 − 0.40) = 12.1%.

C is incorrect. 20.2% is the ROE. The last step, multiplying by the retention rate, was skipped.

BA II Plus: 0.7 × 0.8 × 0.15 × 1.2 × 2 = 0.2016; × 0.6 = 0.1210.

questions.concept: Pro forma modelling, CFO indirect method and equity roll-forward
questions.stem: An industrial company reports the following (in ¥ millions): retained earnings of 800 at the start and 870 at the end of the year; net income of 190; dividends payable of 35 at the start and 15 at the end of the year. All dividends declared flow through dividends payable. Cash dividends paid in the financing section of the cash flow statement are closest to:

options.A: ¥100 million
options.B: ¥120 million
options.C: ¥140 million

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. ¥100 million subtracts the 20 decline in payable from declared dividends. A decrease in a liability means cash paid exceeds the expense, so it must be added.

B is incorrect. ¥120 million is the dividends declared; the change in dividends payable was ignored.

C is correct. Roll-forward of retained earnings: dividends declared = 800 + 190 − 870 = 120. Dividends payable fell by 20, so more cash was paid than declared: cash paid = 120 + 20 = ¥140 million.

BA II Plus: 800 + 190 − 870 = 120; 120 + (35 − 15) = 140.

questions.concept: Leases (lessee view) and long-term liabilities
questions.stem: Helio plc and Ortho Inc. each sign an identical five-year equipment lease with the same payments. Helio reports under IFRS 16. Ortho reports under US GAAP and classifies the lease as an operating lease. Compared with Ortho, Helio will most likely report in the first year:

options.A: higher EBITDA and lower cash flow from operations.
options.B: lower total lease-related expense and lower reported liabilities.
options.C: higher EBITDA and higher cash flow from operations.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. EBITDA is higher, but CFO is not lower. Only the interest portion could remain in CFO under IFRS; the principal repayment moves to financing, so CFO is higher.

B is incorrect. The IFRS 16 method front-loads expense (interest is highest early on), so total expense in the early years is higher, not lower. Both approaches put the lease liability on the balance sheet, so liabilities are not lower.

C is correct. Under IFRS 16 the lessee reports depreciation and interest on the lease; both are below EBITDA, so EBITDA is higher than under US GAAP, where a single straight-line operating lease expense is deducted within operating expenses. The principal portion of the payment is a financing outflow under IFRS 16, whereas the whole payment is operating under a US GAAP operating lease, so CFO is higher under IFRS.

questions.concept: Pensions: DB assumptions, OCI vs P&L
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about defined benefit pension reporting is least accurate?

options.A: Under IFRS, current service cost is recognised in profit or loss.
options.B: Under US GAAP, pension expense in profit or loss includes the actual return on plan assets.
options.C: Under IFRS, remeasurements of the net pension liability are recognised in other comprehensive income and not later reclassified to profit or loss.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Accurate. Current service cost is part of employee benefit expense in profit or loss under IFRS (and also in US GAAP).

B is correct. US GAAP includes the expected return on plan assets in periodic pension cost; the difference between actual and expected return goes to OCI (and may be amortised into profit or loss later). The statement is false.

C is incorrect. Accurate. IFRS recognises remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses and the difference between actual return on assets and the interest income on assets) in OCI; they are not amortised or recycled through profit or loss.

questions.concept: Bond issuance, effective interest amortisation, debt covenants (long-term liabilities)
questions.stem: On 1 January a company issues CHF 1,000,000 face value of five-year bonds with an annual coupon of 6%, paid at each year-end. The market yield at issuance is 8%. Under the effective interest method, the carrying amount of the bonds immediately after the first coupon payment is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. CHF 920,146 is the issue price, i.e. no amortisation of the discount. The carrying amount of a discount bond rises toward face value each period.

B is correct. Issue price = PV of 5 coupons of 60,000 and 1,000,000 at 8% = CHF 920,146. Year 1 interest expense = 920,146 × 8% = 73,612; coupon paid = 60,000; discount amortised = 13,612. Carrying amount = 920,146 + 13,612 = CHF 933,757.

C is incorrect. CHF 936,117 uses straight-line amortisation of the discount (79,854 / 5 = 15,971). The effective interest method amortises less in the early years.

BA II Plus: N = 5, I/Y = 8, PMT = 60,000, FV = 1,000,000, CPT PV = −920,145.80. Then 920,145.80 × 1.08 − 60,000 = 933,757.46.

questions.concept: Income statement: non-recurring items, discontinued ops, OCI, comprehensive income
questions.stem: A company reports the following for the year (in € millions): income from continuing operations, net of tax, 400; loss from discontinued operations, net of tax, 60; unrealised gain on debt securities measured at fair value through OCI, 30; foreign currency translation loss, 45; dividends paid, 100. Total comprehensive income is:

options.A: €225 million
options.B: €325 million
options.C: €385 million

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. €225 million deducts dividends paid. Dividends are a distribution to owners and are not part of comprehensive income.

B is correct. Net income = 400 − 60 = 340 (discontinued operations are part of net income). OCI = +30 − 45 = −15. Comprehensive income = 340 − 15 = €325 million.

C is incorrect. €385 million leaves out the discontinued operations loss. Although non-recurring, it is included in net income and therefore in comprehensive income.

BA II Plus: 400 − 60 + 30 − 45 = 325.

questions.concept: Cash flow statement: direct method, IFRS vs US GAAP classification
questions.stem: Compared with IFRS, US GAAP most likely:

options.A: permits dividends paid to be classified as an operating cash flow.
options.B: permits interest received to be classified as an investing cash flow.
options.C: requires interest paid to be classified as an operating cash flow.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. This is an IFRS option. US GAAP requires dividends paid to be a financing cash flow.

B is incorrect. This is an IFRS option (interest and dividends received in operating or investing). US GAAP requires interest received to be operating.

C is correct. US GAAP requires interest paid, interest received and dividends received to be operating cash flows and dividends paid to be financing. IFRS allows interest paid in operating or financing activities.

questions.concept: Financial reporting quality: earnings quality spectrum, warning signs
questions.stem: An analyst finds that Brenner Inc.'s financial statements comply with applicable accounting standards and are decision-useful, but this year's earnings include a large gain on the sale of a plant that will not recur. Brenner's results are best described as:

options.A: high-quality reporting with low-quality earnings.
options.B: low-quality reporting with high-quality earnings.
options.C: low-quality reporting with low-quality earnings.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Reporting quality refers to compliance and decision-usefulness (satisfied here). Earnings quality refers to whether earnings are sustainable and reflect adequate returns; a non-recurring gain is not sustainable, so earnings quality is low.

B is incorrect. The reverse of the situation: the reporting is compliant and useful, and the earnings are not sustainable.

C is incorrect. The reporting itself is compliant and decision-useful, so reporting quality is high. Only the earnings are low quality.

questions.concept: Activity and liquidity ratios: DSO, DIO, turnover, cash conversion cycle calc
questions.stem: A company reports annual revenue of €4,800 thousand and cost of goods sold of €3,200 thousand. Average accounts receivable are €400 thousand, average inventory €480 thousand and average accounts payable €320 thousand. Using a 365-day year, the cash conversion cycle is closest to:

options.A: 42.6 days
options.B: 48.7 days
options.C: 121.7 days

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. 42.6 days uses revenue instead of COGS for DIO and DPO (36.5 and 24.3 days). Inventory and payables relate to COGS.

B is correct. DSO = 400 / 4,800 × 365 = 30.4 days (revenue basis). DIO = 480 / 3,200 × 365 = 54.8 days and DPO = 320 / 3,200 × 365 = 36.5 days (COGS basis). CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 30.4 + 54.8 − 36.5 = 48.7 days.

C is incorrect. 121.7 days adds DPO instead of subtracting it. Payables days are a source of financing and shorten the cycle.

BA II Plus: 400 ÷ 4,800 × 365 = 30.42; 480 ÷ 3,200 × 365 = 54.75; 320 ÷ 3,200 × 365 = 36.50; 30.42 + 54.75 − 36.50 = 48.67.

questions.concept: Balance sheet: intangibles, goodwill impairment, equity components, treasury stock
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about goodwill is least accurate?

options.A: Goodwill is not amortised but is tested for impairment at least annually.
options.B: Under IFRS, a goodwill impairment loss may be reversed if the recoverable amount of the cash-generating unit later recovers.
options.C: A goodwill impairment loss reduces net income but has no direct effect on cash flow.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Accurate. Acquired goodwill is carried at cost less impairment and tested at least annually (at the cash-generating unit level under IFRS, the reporting unit under US GAAP).

B is correct. Neither IFRS nor US GAAP allows reversal of a goodwill impairment loss. (IFRS permits reversal for other assets, but not for goodwill.) This statement is false.

C is incorrect. Accurate. The impairment is a non-cash charge: net income and equity fall, but cash flow from operations is unaffected (it is added back in the indirect method).

questions.concept: Expense recognition: depreciation methods, warranties, bad debts
questions.stem: A company buys equipment for $90,000 with an estimated residual value of $10,000 and a five-year useful life, and uses the double-declining balance method. Depreciation expense in the second year is:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. $14,400 applies 40% to the first-year depreciation (36,000 × 40%) rather than to the beginning carrying amount.

B is incorrect. $19,200 deducts the residual value before applying DDB: (80,000 − 32,000) × 40%. DDB applies to the carrying amount without subtracting salvage.

C is correct. DDB rate = 2 × (1/5) = 40% of beginning carrying amount (residual ignored until the end). Year 1: 90,000 × 40% = 36,000. Year 2: (90,000 − 36,000) × 40% = $21,600.

BA II Plus: 90,000 × 0.4 = 36,000; (90,000 − 36,000) × 0.4 = 21,600.

questions.concept: Real options: identify timing, sizing, abandonment, flexibility, fundamental options
questions.stem: Caldera Energy is evaluating a lease on an offshore oil field. Once developed, the field's profitability depends almost entirely on the market price of oil: if prices are high the project is highly valuable, and if they stay low the project has little value. The cash flows resemble the payoff of an option on the price of oil, and the company has no ability to defer, resize or abandon the project once it has begun. The project is best described as containing a:

options.A: fundamental option.
options.B: timing option.
options.C: flexibility option.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A fundamental option arises when the project itself is an option on an underlying asset, such as an oil or mineral project whose payoff depends on the commodity price. Its value derives from the underlying price, not from management actions during the project.

B is incorrect. A timing option involves the ability to delay investment to gain information. The stem rules out deferral.

C is incorrect. Flexibility options (price-setting and production-flexibility options) involve management changing prices or output in response to conditions. The stem rules out management intervention.

questions.concept: Capital allocation: NPV vs IRR conflicts, ROIC vs WACC, share-price NPV, project categories
questions.stem:
A company with a weighted average cost of capital of 9% must choose between two mutually exclusive projects with the following cash flows (in $ thousands):

ProjectYear 0Year 1Year 2Year 3
X−300200200100
Y−900300400700

The company should most appropriately choose:

options.A: Project X, because it has the higher IRR.
options.B: Project X, because it has the higher profitability index.
options.C: Project Y, because it has the higher NPV.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. IRR of X is about 34.6% versus about 22.0% for Y, so IRR ranks X first. IRR ignores project scale and can conflict with NPV for mutually exclusive projects; NPV wins.

B is incorrect. PI = 1 + NPV / outlay is 1.43 for X versus 1.28 for Y. Like IRR, PI is a ratio that ignores the scale of the investment and can rank mutually exclusive projects differently from NPV.

C is correct. NPV of X at 9% = $129.0 thousand; NPV of Y = $252.4 thousand. For mutually exclusive projects, NPV measures the increase in shareholder wealth and is the correct criterion when rankings conflict. Y adds more value even though it is larger and has a lower IRR.

BA II Plus: CF0 = −300, C01 = 200, F01 = 2 (or enter each year), C02 = 100, then NPV, I = 9, CPT = 129.04. Repeat for Y: −900, 300, 400, 700 gives NPV = 252.43. IRR CPT: X = 34.6%, Y = 22.0%.

questions.concept: Capital allocation: NPV vs IRR conflicts, ROIC vs WACC, share-price NPV, project categories
questions.stem: Torvik SE has 40 million shares outstanding trading at €25.00. It announces a new project that investors had not anticipated, with an NPV of €60 million. Assuming the market is efficient and the NPV is the only new information, the share price should rise to:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. The price would be unchanged only if the market had already anticipated the project and priced it in. The stem says it was not anticipated.

B is correct. The NPV accrues to existing shareholders: €60 million / 40 million shares = €1.50 per share. New price = 25.00 + 1.50 = €26.50.

C is incorrect. €85.00 adds the whole NPV in millions (60) to the per-share price without dividing by the number of shares.

BA II Plus: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.50; 25 + 1.50 = 26.50.

questions.concept: WACC with target D/E weights, marginal tax, project risk adjustment
questions.stem: A company targets a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.6. Its pre-tax cost of debt is 6%, its marginal tax rate is 25% (its average tax rate is 20%), the risk-free rate is 3%, its equity beta is 1.1 and the equity risk premium is 5.5%. Its weighted average cost of capital is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. 6.32% treats D/E as the weight on debt and uses 0.4 for equity: 0.6 × 4.5% + 0.4 × 9.05%. D/E must first be converted to D/V.

B is correct. D/E = 0.6 means D/V = 0.6 / 1.6 = 37.5% and E/V = 62.5%. Cost of equity = 3% + 1.1 × 5.5% = 9.05%. WACC = 0.375 × 6% × (1 − 0.25) + 0.625 × 9.05% = 1.69% + 5.66% = 7.34%.

C is incorrect. 7.91% omits the interest tax shield: 0.375 × 6% + 0.625 × 9.05%. The after-tax cost of debt must be used.

BA II Plus: 1 + 0.6 = 1.6; 0.6 ÷ 1.6 = 0.375; 6 × 0.75 = 4.5; 0.375 × 4.5 + 0.625 × 9.05 = 7.34.

questions.concept: Liquidity: primary vs secondary sources, drags vs pulls, factoring, cash conversion cycle
questions.stem: Zenith Corp.'s treasurer reports two developments: (1) customers are paying later than the agreed terms, and (2) suppliers have shortened their credit terms from 60 to 30 days. These developments are most likely, respectively:

options.A: a drag on liquidity and a pull on liquidity.
options.B: a pull on liquidity and a drag on liquidity.
options.C: both pulls on liquidity.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Drags delay cash inflows (slow receivables, obsolete inventory, bad debts). Pulls accelerate cash outflows (shortened payables terms, lower credit limits, margin calls). Late-paying customers are a drag; shorter supplier terms are a pull.

B is incorrect. The classification is reversed. Slow collections delay inflows (drag) and shorter supplier terms accelerate outflows (pull).

C is incorrect. Late customer payments do not speed up outflows; they delay inflows, which is a drag.

questions.concept: Liquidity: primary vs secondary sources, drags vs pulls, factoring, cash conversion cycle
questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a secondary source of liquidity?

options.A: Negotiating a change to the terms of existing debt contracts.
options.B: Selling a non-core division.
options.C: Drawing on a committed bank line of credit.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Secondary source: renegotiating debt contracts (for example, covenants or maturities) is a way to relieve liquidity strain and can signal financial distress.

B is incorrect. Secondary source: liquidating assets is a typical secondary source and may affect operations and signal weakness.

C is correct. Ready cash, cash flow from operations and short-term funding such as committed credit lines and trade credit are primary sources. A drawn committed line is a primary source of liquidity.

questions.concept: Governance and agency: stakeholder vs shareholder theory, pay structures
questions.stem: The board of a listed manufacturer wants to reduce the agency conflict between executives and shareholders, including short-term risk taking. Which compensation structure would most likely achieve this?

options.A: Restricted shares that vest over five years, with clawback provisions tied to long-term performance.
options.B: A large annual cash bonus based on revenue growth.
options.C: A fixed salary only, with no variable pay.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Multi-year vesting aligns executives with long-term shareholder value, and clawback discourages excessive short-term risk taking and misreporting.

B is incorrect. An annual bonus on revenue growth encourages short-termism and growth at the expense of profitability, which worsens the agency conflict.

C is incorrect. With only fixed pay, managers bear no outcome-based incentive, and may be risk-averse or complacent; there is no alignment with shareholders.

questions.concept: Capital structure: static trade-off, why leverage below optimum, start-up financing
questions.stem: At its current level of debt, the marginal benefit of the interest tax shield for Delmar Ltd. exceeds the present value of the marginal expected costs of financial distress. Under static trade-off theory, Delmar:

options.A: is at its optimal capital structure, so changing debt will not affect firm value.
options.B: is over-levered, and reducing debt would increase firm value.
options.C: is under-levered, and adding debt would increase firm value.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. The optimum is where the marginal benefit equals the marginal cost. Here the benefit is larger, so the optimum has not been reached.

B is incorrect. Over-leverage would mean the marginal distress cost exceeds the marginal tax benefit. The stem states the opposite.

C is correct. Firm value = value if unlevered + PV of tax shield − PV of expected distress costs. While the marginal tax benefit exceeds the marginal expected distress cost, each additional unit of debt raises firm value, so the firm is below its optimal leverage.

questions.concept: Business models: value chain, pricing strategies; public vs private issuers and double taxation
questions.stem: A publicly traded corporation in a jurisdiction with a classical double-taxation system earns €1,000,000 of profit before tax. The corporate tax rate is 25%, the company distributes all after-tax profit as dividends, and shareholders pay a 20% tax on dividends received. The total amount that shareholders retain after all taxes is:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. €550,000 adds the two tax rates (25% + 20% = 45%) and applies them to the pre-tax profit. The dividend tax applies to the after-corporate-tax amount.

B is correct. Profit after corporate tax = 1,000,000 × 0.75 = 750,000. Dividends are taxed again: 750,000 × 0.80 = €600,000. The combined burden is 40%, not 45%.

C is incorrect. €750,000 ignores the second layer of tax at the shareholder level.

BA II Plus: 1,000,000 × 0.75 = 750,000; 750,000 × 0.80 = 600,000.

questions.concept: Organisational forms, stakeholder groups and conflicts (shareholders vs creditors)
questions.stem: Which of the following management actions, taken in the interest of shareholders, would most likely be detrimental to creditors?

options.A: Issuing new equity to repay existing debt.
options.B: Paying a large special dividend financed by selling assets.
options.C: Retaining earnings to fund low-risk investments.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Using equity proceeds to repay debt strengthens the creditors' position.

B is correct. A debt-financed or asset-funded special dividend transfers value from creditors to shareholders: collateral and the equity cushion shrink while claims on the firm are unchanged. This is a classic shareholder-creditor conflict.

C is incorrect. Retaining earnings for low-risk investments raises the equity cushion and reduces risk for creditors.

questions.concept: Working capital management and short-term funding sources
questions.stem: Compared with an uncommitted line of credit, a committed line of credit with a bank will most likely:

options.A: involve a commitment fee but legally oblige the bank to lend up to the limit.
options.B: carry no fees but allow the bank to refuse to lend if conditions change.
options.C: be available only to issuers with the highest credit ratings, and it is unsecured.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A committed line (a formal agreement) charges a fee on the unused portion and obliges the bank to provide funds, subject to conditions. It is a more reliable primary source of liquidity.

B is incorrect. This describes an uncommitted line: usually no commitment fee, but the bank has no obligation to lend.

C is incorrect. Commercial paper, not bank credit lines, is restricted to high-rated issuers. Committed lines are available to a broader range of firms and may be secured or unsecured.

questions.concept: ESG factors and integration; green finance
questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely classified as a governance factor in ESG analysis?

options.A: Board independence.
options.B: Executive remuneration structure.
options.C: Employee health and safety record.

questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. Governance: board composition and independence.

B is incorrect. Governance: executive remuneration and its alignment with shareholders.

C is correct. Employee health and safety is a social factor (labour practices and human capital).

questions.concept: Operating and financial leverage, payback and profitability index
questions.stem: A company has annual sales of $5,000 thousand, variable operating costs of $3,000 thousand, fixed operating costs of $1,000 thousand and interest expense of $200 thousand. Variable costs move in proportion to sales and the tax rate is constant. If sales increase by 10%, net income will most likely increase by:
questions.explanation:
A is incorrect. 12.5% uses only DFL (1.25 × 10%), ignoring operating leverage.

B is incorrect. 20% = DOL × 10% only, which is the change in EBIT. Financial leverage then magnifies the change in net income.

C is correct. Contribution margin = 5,000 − 3,000 = 2,000. EBIT = 2,000 − 1,000 = 1,000. DOL = 2,000 / 1,000 = 2.0. DFL = EBIT / (EBIT − interest) = 1,000 / 800 = 1.25. DTL = 2.0 × 1.25 = 2.5; net income rises 10% × 2.5 = 25%.

BA II Plus: 2,000 ÷ 1,000 = 2.0; 1,000 ÷ 800 = 1.25; 2.0 × 1.25 = 2.5.

questions.concept: DDM: multistage (D_n+1 at year n), delayed first dividend, model selection, preferred valuation
questions.stem:
Halvorsen Marine Ltd paid an annual dividend of USD 1.50 per share yesterday. Analysts expect dividends to grow 10% a year for the next three years and 3% a year indefinitely thereafter. The required return on equity is 8%.

The value of a share today is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Dividends: D1 = 1.50 × 1.10 = 1.650; D2 = 1.815; D3 = 1.9965. First dividend of the stable stage: D4 = 1.9965 × 1.03 = 2.0564.

V3 = D4 / (r − g) = 2.0564 / 0.05 = 41.128 (value at the end of year 3).

V0 = 1.650/1.08 + 1.815/1.082 + (1.9965 + 41.128)/1.083 = 1.528 + 1.556 + 34.233 = USD 37.32.

BA II Plus: [CF] [2nd][CLR WORK]; CF0 = 0 [ENTER]; C01 = 1.65 ; C02 = 1.815 ; C03 = 43.1244 (= 1.9965 + 41.128); [NPV] I = 8 [ENTER] [↓] [CPT] = 37.32.

LOS: multistage DDM — the terminal value at year n uses Dn+1 and is discounted n periods, plus Dn in year n.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — Uses D3 instead of D4 in the terminal value: 1.9965/0.05 = 39.93, then PV = 1.528 + 1.556 + (1.9965 + 39.93)/1.083 = 36.37. The Gordon step must use the first dividend of the new growth rate, Dn+1.
  • C — Discounts the terminal value four periods instead of three: V3/1.084 = 41.128/1.3605 = 30.23, plus PV(D1..D3) = 1.528 + 1.556 + 1.585 = 4.669, total 34.90. V3 is a value at t = 3 (one period before D4), so it is discounted three periods.

questions.concept: DDM: multistage (D_n+1 at year n), delayed first dividend, model selection, preferred valuation
questions.stem:
Brightwater Biotech pays no dividend today. Management states that the first annual dividend, EUR 2.40 per share, will be paid exactly four years from today (t = 4), and dividends will grow at 5% a year thereafter. The required return on equity is 10%.

The value of a share today is closest to:
questions.explanation:
The Gordon model values the share one period before the first dividend: V3 = D4 / (r − g) = 2.40 / (0.10 − 0.05) = 48.00.

V0 = 48.00 / 1.103 = EUR 36.06.

BA II Plus: 48 [÷] 1.1 [yx] 3 [=] 36.06.

LOS: delayed-dividend / multistage DDM — discount the Gordon value n periods where Dn+1 is the first dividend.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Discounts 4 periods (48.00/1.104 = 32.78): treats the Gordon value as being at t = 4, the date of the first dividend, rather than one year before it.
  • C — Grows the first dividend again (2.40 × 1.05 = 2.52; 2.52/0.05 = 50.40; /1.331 = 37.87). The EUR 2.40 already is D4, the first dividend of the growth phase.

questions.concept: DDM: multistage (D_n+1 at year n), delayed first dividend, model selection, preferred valuation
questions.stem: Which of the following companies is LEAST suited to valuation with the constant-growth (Gordon) dividend discount model?

options.A: A mature regulated water utility paying stable dividends that grow with inflation
options.B: A consumer-staples company with a stable 60% payout ratio, steady ROE and long-run growth of 3%
options.C: Nexa Software, which pays no dividend, is growing earnings 25% a year, and expects to start paying dividends in six years

questions.explanation:
The Gordon model needs dividends that are paid now (or soon), growing at a stable rate below the required return indefinitely. A fast-growing firm with no dividend and a very different future growth pattern needs a multistage (or delayed-dividend) model, or a model that does not depend on dividends (FCFE, residual income, multiples).

LOS: select the appropriate dividend discount model.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — The utility has stable, inflation-linked growth: a textbook Gordon candidate.
  • B — The staples firm has a stable payout, steady ROE and moderate growth: suited to Gordon.

questions.concept: Equity indexes: price vs total return index, weighting methods, reconstitution, multi-market
questions.stem:
An analyst tracks a three-stock market with the data below (no dividends, no splits).

StockPrice at start (USD)Price at end (USD)Shares outstanding (m)
X808440
Y202410
Z504530

The return on an equal-weighted index of the three stocks is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Individual returns: X = 84/80 − 1 = +5.0%; Y = 24/20 − 1 = +20.0%; Z = 45/50 − 1 = −10.0%.

Equal-weighted index return = simple average = (5 + 20 − 10)/3 = 5.0%.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 2.0% is the price-weighted return: (84 + 24 + 45)/(80 + 20 + 50) − 1 = 153/150 − 1. Higher-priced stocks get more weight, not equal weight.
  • C — 1.0% is the value-weighted return: market caps 3,200 + 200 + 1,500 = 4,900 rise to 3,360 + 240 + 1,350 = 4,950, i.e. +1.02%.

questions.concept: Equity indexes: price vs total return index, weighting methods, reconstitution, multi-market
questions.stem:
At the start of the year the price return index of a large-cap equity market stood at 1,500 and the total return index at 2,400. During the year the price return index rose to 1,590. The constituents paid dividends equal to 36 index points over the year, received at year-end and not reinvested earlier.

The total return index at the end of the year is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Total return for the year = (price change + dividends)/starting price index = (1,590 − 1,500 + 36)/1,500 = 126/1,500 = 8.4%.

The total return index is grown by that return: 2,400 × 1.084 = 2,601.6.

Price return alone is 6.0%; the dividend adds 2.4%.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 2,544.0 grows the total return index by the price return only (6.0%), ignoring dividends.
  • B — 2,526.0 adds index points from the price index to the total return index level (2,400 + 90 + 36). The two indexes are on different bases; apply the percentage return instead.

questions.concept: Justified P/E, P/B and P/S relationships; sustainable growth rate
questions.stem:
Calder Foods earns a steady return on equity of 12% and pays out 60% of earnings as dividends. Its required return on equity is 9%, and the growth rate can be assumed sustainable and constant.

The justified trailing P/E is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Sustainable growth g = retention × ROE = (1 − 0.60) × 12% = 4.8%.

Justified leading P/E = payout/(r − g) = 0.60/(0.09 − 0.048) = 14.29.

Trailing P/E = leading × (1 + g) = 14.29 × 1.048 = 14.97 ≈ 15.0 (equivalently D0/E0 × (1+g)/(r−g)).

Why the others are wrong

  • B — 14.3 is the justified leading (forward) P/E, P0/E1; the question asks for trailing.
  • C — 33.3 uses g = payout × ROE = 7.2% (instead of retention × ROE): 0.60/(0.09 − 0.072) = 33.3.

questions.concept: Justified P/E, P/B and P/S relationships; sustainable growth rate
questions.stem: A bank has an expected sustainable ROE of 14%, a required return on equity of 9%, and a constant growth rate of 5%. Its justified price-to-book ratio is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Justified P/B = (ROE − g)/(r − g) = (0.14 − 0.05)/(0.09 − 0.05) = 0.09/0.04 = 2.25.

Check: = 1 + (ROE − r)/(r − g) = 1 + 0.05/0.04.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 1.25 is only the premium over book, (ROE − r)/(r − g); the 1 for the book value itself is missing.
  • C — 3.50 divides ROE by (r − g) = 0.14/0.04, forgetting to subtract g in the numerator.

questions.concept: Company and industry analysis: PESTLE, five forces, revenue drivers, working capital and PP&E forecasts
questions.stem:
Orsini Packaging forecasts sales of EUR 2,000m next year. Capital expenditure is projected at 6% of sales and depreciation at 8% of beginning net PP&E. Beginning net PP&E is EUR 800m and there are no disposals.

Forecast end-of-year net PP&E is closest to:

options.A: EUR 984m
options.B: EUR 736m
options.C: EUR 856m

questions.explanation:
Capex = 6% × 2,000 = 120. Depreciation = 8% × 800 = 64.

Ending net PP&E = beginning + capex − depreciation = 800 + 120 − 64 = EUR 856m.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 984 adds depreciation instead of subtracting it (800 + 120 + 64).
  • B — 736 omits capex (800 − 64): net PP&E falls only by depreciation if nothing is invested.

questions.concept: Company and industry analysis: PESTLE, five forces, revenue drivers, working capital and PP&E forecasts
questions.stem:
An analyst forecasts sales of EUR 3,650m for Veldt Industrial. COGS is 60% of sales. Assumptions (365-day year): days sales outstanding 45, days inventory on hand 60, days payables outstanding 30.

Forecast operating working capital (receivables + inventory − payables) is closest to:

options.A: EUR 630m
options.B: EUR 750m
options.C: EUR 990m

questions.explanation:
COGS = 0.60 × 3,650 = 2,190.

Receivables = 3,650 × 45/365 = 450. Inventory = 2,190 × 60/365 = 360. Payables = 2,190 × 30/365 = 180.

Operating working capital = 450 + 360 − 180 = EUR 630m.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — 750 drives inventory (600) and payables (300) off sales instead of COGS: 450 + 600 − 300.
  • C — 990 adds payables instead of subtracting them: 450 + 360 + 180.

questions.concept: Company and industry analysis: PESTLE, five forces, revenue drivers, working capital and PP&E forecasts
questions.stem: Using Porter's five forces, which of the following is LEAST likely to increase rivalry among existing competitors in an industry?

options.A: High exit barriers
options.B: Rapid growth in industry demand
options.C: Competitors of similar size selling largely undifferentiated products

questions.explanation:
Rivalry intensifies when growth is slow (firms gain share only by taking it from rivals), exit barriers keep excess capacity in the industry, and competitors are similar in size with little differentiation. Rapid demand growth lets all firms expand without taking share from others, so it eases rivalry.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — High exit barriers keep marginal firms and excess capacity in the industry: raises rivalry.
  • C — Similar-sized rivals with undifferentiated products compete on price: raises rivalry.

questions.concept: Order types, trade execution, short selling, margin calls and leverage ratio
questions.stem:
An investor buys 1,000 shares of Tessin Instruments at CHF 40 using 50% initial margin and borrows the rest. The maintenance margin requirement is 30%. Ignore interest and dividends.

The share price at which the investor first receives a margin call is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Loan = 0.50 × 40 × 1,000 = CHF 20,000 (CHF 20 per share). Equity % = (P − 20)/P. Margin call when (P − 20)/P = 0.30 ⇒ P = 20/(1 − 0.30) = CHF 28.57.

Equivalent: P0 × (1 − initial margin)/(1 − maintenance margin) = 40 × 0.50/0.70.

BA II Plus: 40 [×] 0.5 [÷] 0.7 [=] 28.57.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — 28.00 is 40 × (1 − 0.30): applies the maintenance margin to the purchase price, ignoring that the CHF 20 loan stays fixed.
  • C — 46.15 is the short-sale formula P0(1 + IM)/(1 + MM) = 40 × 1.5/1.3; a long position is called when the price falls, not rises.

questions.concept: Order types, trade execution, short selling, margin calls and leverage ratio
questions.stem:
An investor sells short 1,000 shares of Norvik Retail at USD 50, with an initial margin of 50% (USD 25,000 of the investor's own equity is deposited). While the position is open, Norvik pays a dividend of USD 1.50 per share. The investor then buys the shares back at USD 44. Ignore interest on the margin account and commissions.

The return on the investor's initial equity is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Gain from price fall = (50 − 44) × 1,000 = 6,000. The short seller must reimburse the dividend: 1.50 × 1,000 = 1,500.

Net profit = 6,000 − 1,500 = 4,500. Return on equity = 4,500/25,000 = 18.0%.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 24.0% is 6,000/25,000: ignores the dividend the short seller owes the lender.
  • B — 30.0% adds the dividend (7,500/25,000) instead of deducting it; a short seller pays dividends, never receives them.

questions.concept: Market efficiency and anomalies: semi-strong implications, momentum, size effect
questions.stem: Assume the equity market is semi-strong form efficient but not strong form efficient, and ignore legal constraints. Which strategy is MOST likely to produce consistent abnormal returns after costs?

options.A: Buying shares immediately after a positive quarterly earnings surprise is announced
options.B: Trading on confidential knowledge, held by a few executives, of an unannounced takeover bid
options.C: Screening financial statements for stocks with low P/E ratios and holding them

questions.explanation:
Semi-strong efficiency means prices already reflect all public information (past prices and published financial data), so neither fundamental analysis of public data nor reacting to announcements should earn abnormal returns. Only private (inside) information is not yet reflected, which is the condition ruled out by the strong form.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — An earnings announcement is public; prices adjust at once, so buying afterwards earns only the normal return.
  • C — P/E screens use public information; under semi-strong efficiency they cannot earn consistent abnormal returns.

questions.concept: Market efficiency and anomalies: semi-strong implications, momentum, size effect
questions.stem: Which statement about market anomalies is LEAST accurate?

options.A: Many anomalies weaken or disappear after they are widely publicized, consistent with investors trading them away
options.B: Apparent anomalies can arise because the asset pricing model used to measure risk-adjusted returns is wrong (the joint-hypothesis problem)
options.C: An anomaly that is statistically significant in a single sample period is sufficient proof that the market is inefficient

questions.explanation:
One significant sample is not proof: results may come from data mining, chance, risk mis-measurement or transaction costs that make the strategy unprofitable. Anomalies must persist out of sample, after costs and risk adjustment, before they point to inefficiency.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Accurate: disappearance after publication is a common finding (e.g. size effect weakening).
  • B — Accurate: tests of efficiency are joint tests of efficiency and the pricing model.

questions.concept: Stock dividends, ADR/GRS types, preference shares
questions.stem: An investor owns 1,000 shares of Lindqvist AB, priced at EUR 33.00. The company declares a 10% stock dividend. All else equal, the value of the investor's holding immediately after the stock dividend is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A stock dividend splits ownership into more shares without changing the company's assets or total value. Holding becomes 1,100 shares; the price adjusts to 33.00/1.10 = 30.00. Value = 1,100 × 30.00 = EUR 33,000, unchanged.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — 36,300 = 1,100 × 33: assumes the price stays unchanged, so wealth rises 10%. A stock dividend creates no wealth.
  • C — 30,000 = 1,000 × 30: uses the new price but the old number of shares.

questions.concept: Stock dividends, ADR/GRS types, preference shares
questions.stem: A Taiwanese semiconductor company wants to list on a major US exchange and, at the same time, sell newly issued shares to US investors through a public offering. Which depositary receipt structure is required?

options.A: Sponsored Level I ADR
options.B: Sponsored Level III ADR
options.C: Sponsored Level II ADR

questions.explanation:
Level III is the only level that can raise new capital in a US public offering; it requires full SEC registration and exchange listing. Level I trades over the counter with minimal disclosure and no capital raising; Level II lists existing shares on an exchange but cannot raise capital.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Level I: OTC, minimal SEC disclosure; cannot raise capital.
  • C — Level II: exchange listing of existing shares only, no new capital.

questions.concept: Equity security types and risks; depositary receipts vs common vs private equity
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about preference shares is LEAST accurate?

options.A: They typically pay a fixed dividend
options.B: They rank ahead of common shares in claims on assets in liquidation
options.C: Preference shareholders normally have the same voting rights as common shareholders

questions.explanation:
Preference shares usually carry no (or limited) voting rights; in exchange they receive a fixed dividend and rank ahead of common shareholders on dividends and liquidation.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Accurate: dividends are usually fixed at a stated rate.
  • B — Accurate: preference shares have a senior claim to common equity.

questions.concept: Primary vs secondary markets, IPOs and securities offerings
questions.stem: Meridian Logistics, already listed, wants to file one registration statement and then sell shares in several tranches over the next 24 months as market conditions allow. This offering mechanism is best described as a:

options.A: shelf registration
options.B: private placement
options.C: rights offering

questions.explanation:
A shelf registration lets an issuer register securities once and sell them in portions over time, reducing delay and cost.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — A private placement sells to a small group of investors without a public registration.
  • C — A rights offering offers new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

questions.concept: Residual income and asset-based valuation
questions.stem:
Sorell AG has a book value of EUR 40.00 per share and expected EPS of EUR 4.80 next year. The required return on equity is 9%. Residual income is expected to stay at its first-year level in perpetuity.

The intrinsic value per share is closest to:
questions.explanation:
RI1 = EPS − r × B0 = 4.80 − 0.09 × 40.00 = 1.20.

V0 = B0 + RI/r = 40.00 + 1.20/0.09 = 40.00 + 13.33 = EUR 53.33.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 41.20 = B0 + RI1: adds one year of residual income instead of capitalizing it as a perpetuity.
  • C — 13.33 is only the PV of the residual income; the book value is missing.

questions.concept: Enterprise value multiples: EV/EBITDA, P/S comparisons
questions.stem: Pelham Chemicals has a market capitalization of USD 800m, debt of USD 300m, preferred shares of USD 50m and cash of USD 100m. EBITDA is USD 150m. Its EV/EBITDA is closest to:
questions.explanation:
EV = market cap + debt + preferred − cash = 800 + 300 + 50 − 100 = 1,050. EV/EBITDA = 1,050/150 = 7.00.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 8.33 adds cash (1,250/150) instead of subtracting it.
  • B — 6.67 omits the preferred shares (1,000/150); preferred is part of enterprise value.

questions.concept: Industry life cycle and competitive strategy positioning
questions.stem: In one industry, growth has slowed sharply, capacity exceeds demand, price competition is intense and weaker firms are being forced to exit. Which stage of the industry life cycle is this?

options.A: Shakeout
options.B: Mature
options.C: Growth

questions.explanation:
Shakeout: slowing growth and overcapacity cause price competition, falling profits and exits of weak firms. Mature: slow stable growth with a consolidated set of survivors. Growth: rapid expansion with new entrants.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — Mature is a stabilised stage after the weak firms have already left; here exits are still under way.
  • C — Growth has rapid demand expansion and few price wars; here demand growth is slowing.

questions.concept: Contracts, positions, clearing and settlement; financial system functions
questions.stem: Which description best fits settlement of an equity trade?

options.A: Confirming that trade details agree between the two parties
options.B: Transfer of securities to the buyer and cash to the seller after the trade has been matched
options.C: Determining the price at which the security will trade

questions.explanation:
Clearing validates and matches trade details; settlement is the final transfer of ownership and cash.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — That describes confirmation/matching (clearing).
  • C — That is price discovery.

questions.concept: Equity indexes: price-weighted index divisor after a stock split
questions.stem:
A price-weighted index contains three stocks priced at USD 50, USD 30 and USD 20, and the index divisor is 3 (index level 33.33). The USD 50 stock then undergoes a 2-for-1 stock split, and its price adjusts to USD 25. All other prices are unchanged.

To keep the index level unchanged, the new divisor is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Before the split the sum of prices is 50 + 30 + 20 = 100 and the index is 100/3 = 33.33. After the split the sum is 25 + 30 + 20 = 75. To keep the index at 33.33 the new divisor must be 75/33.33 = 2.25.

B is incorrect. Keeping the divisor at 3.00 would let the index fall to 75/3 = 25.00, so the split would wrongly reduce the index even though no value was lost.

C is incorrect. 1.50 = 3/2 divides the old divisor by the split factor. The split only changes one of the three prices, so the divisor must fall proportionally to the change in the sum of prices (75/100), not by the full split factor.

questions.concept: Bond pricing: accrued interest, flat vs full price (30/360, ACT), YTM via BA II Plus BOND worksheet, current yield
questions.stem: A bond pays a 6% coupon semiannually on 15 March and 15 September and matures on 15 September 2031. It is priced to yield 3.9% (stated annual rate, compounded semiannually) for settlement on 12 August 2026. The bond uses the 30/360 day-count convention. The flat (clean) price per 100 of par value is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. From the last coupon (15 March) to settlement (12 August) is 5 × 30 − 3 = 147 days on a 30/360 basis, so accrued interest = 3.00 × 147/180 = 2.45. The fraction of the coupon period remaining is w = (180 − 147)/180 = 0.1833. Discounting the 11 remaining coupons and the redemption at 1.95% per period with the first cash flow at time w gives a full price of 112.06. Flat price = full price − accrued interest = 112.06 − 2.45 = 109.61.

A is incorrect. 112.06 is the full (dirty) price. The question asks for the flat price, so accrued interest must be removed.

C is incorrect. 108.25 discounts the first coupon over 147/180 of a period instead of the 33/180 that remain (the days elapsed were used as the days to the next coupon), then subtracts accrued interest.

BA II Plus: 2nd [BOND] (EUR date format DD.MMYY; to switch, 2nd [FORMAT], scroll to the date line, 2nd [SET] until it shows EUR, then 2nd [QUIT]). SDT = 12.0826 ENTER ↓ CPN = 6 ENTER ↓ RDT = 15.0931 ENTER ↓ RV = 100 ENTER ↓ set 360 (2nd [SET] until it shows 360) ↓ 2/Y ↓ YLD = 3.9 ENTER ↓ CPT PRI = 109.61 (this is the flat price). ↓ AI = 2.45. The full price is PRI + AI = 112.06. Common input slips: wrong RDT year, entering the call/redemption price wrongly, leaving ACT instead of 360.

questions.concept: Bond pricing: accrued interest, flat vs full price (30/360, ACT), YTM via BA II Plus BOND worksheet, current yield
questions.stem: A dealer quotes a flat price of 99.40 per 100 par for a GBP 5,000,000 par holding of a 4% government bond that pays coupons semiannually on 10 January and 10 July. The bond uses the actual/actual day-count convention, and settlement is on 25 May 2027 (there are 181 days between the 10 January and 10 July coupon dates). The amount the buyer pays at settlement is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. The buyer pays the full price = flat price + accrued interest. Days from 10 January to 25 May = 135, and the coupon period has 181 days. Accrued interest = (4%/2) × 135/181 = 2.00 × 0.7459 = 1.4917 per 100. Full price = 99.40 + 1.4917 = 100.8917. Amount = 100.8917% × 5,000,000 = GBP 5,044,586.

A is incorrect. GBP 4,970,000 is the flat price only (99.40% of par). Accrued interest is also paid to the seller.

B is incorrect. GBP 5,119,171 accrues interest on the annual coupon (4.00 × 135/181 = 2.9834) instead of the semiannual coupon of 2.00, which overstates accrued interest.

BA II Plus: 2 × 135 ÷ 181 = 1.4917 (accrued per 100); + 99.40 = 100.8917; × 50,000 = 5,044,586.

questions.concept: Bond pricing: accrued interest, flat vs full price (30/360, ACT), YTM via BA II Plus BOND worksheet, current yield
questions.stem: A bond pays a 5% coupon semiannually on 15 March and 15 September and matures on 15 September 2030. It is quoted at a flat price of 98.70 per 100 of par for settlement on 15 June 2026, using the 30/360 convention. The bond's yield to maturity, stated as an annual rate compounded semiannually, is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Accrued interest = 2.50 × 90/180 = 1.25, so the full price is 98.70 + 1.25 = 99.95. There are 9 coupons remaining and the first is half a period away (w = 0.5). Solving for the semiannual yield that discounts all cash flows to a full price of 99.95 gives 2.6719% per period, or 5.34% annualised.

B is incorrect. 5.07% is the current yield (annual coupon / flat price = 5.00/98.70). It ignores the pull to par and the time to maturity, so it is not a yield to maturity.

C is incorrect. 5.68% treats 98.70 as the full price. That implies a flat price of only 97.45, so the discount to par (and the yield) is overstated.

BA II Plus: 2nd [BOND] (EUR date format DD.MMYY). SDT = 15.0626 ENTER ↓ CPN = 5 ENTER ↓ RDT = 15.0930 ENTER ↓ RV = 100 ↓ 360 ↓ 2/Y ↓ PRI = 98.7 ENTER ↓ CPT YLD = 5.34. Enter the flat price in PRI; the worksheet adds accrued interest itself.

questions.concept: Duration calculations: Macaulay, modified, approximate, portfolio (market-value weights), money duration, annualisation
questions.stem: A bond pays coupons semiannually and has a yield to maturity of 6.0%, stated as an annual rate compounded semiannually. A spreadsheet reports the bond's Macaulay duration as 17.6, measured in semiannual periods. The bond's modified duration, in years, is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. Convert periods to years first: 17.6/2 = 8.80 years. Then ModDur = MacDur/(1 + y/m) = 8.80/(1 + 0.06/2) = 8.80/1.03 = 8.54.

A is incorrect. 17.09 = 17.6/1.03 divides the period-based figure by the periodic factor but never annualises it, so the answer is in periods, not years.

B is incorrect. 8.30 = 8.80/1.06 uses the annual yield as the divisor even though the bond is yield-quoted with semiannual compounding; the divisor must be 1 + 0.06/2.

BA II Plus: 17.6 ÷ 2 = 8.8; ÷ 1.03 = 8.5437.

questions.concept: Duration calculations: Macaulay, modified, approximate, portfolio (market-value weights), money duration, annualisation
questions.stem:
A portfolio manager holds three bonds, shown below. The modified duration of the portfolio is closest to:

BondPar value (EUR)Full price (per 100)Modified duration
X6,000,0001043.0
Y2,000,000956.5
Z2,000,0006212.0
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Portfolio duration is the market-value-weighted average of the bonds' durations. Market values: X = 6,240,000, Y = 1,900,000, Z = 1,240,000; total = 9,380,000. Weights = 0.6652, 0.2026, 0.1322. Duration = 0.6652 × 3.0 + 0.2026 × 6.5 + 0.1322 × 12.0 = 4.90.

B is incorrect. 5.50 weights by par value (60%/20%/20%) instead of market value. Bond Z is trading at 62, so its true weight is much lower than its par weight.

C is incorrect. 7.17 is the simple average of the three durations (equal weights), which ignores position sizes entirely.

BA II Plus: MV weights: 6,240,000 ÷ 9,380,000 = 0.6652, etc. Then 0.6652 × 3 + 0.2026 × 6.5 + 0.1322 × 12 = 4.90.

questions.concept: Duration calculations: Macaulay, modified, approximate, portfolio (market-value weights), money duration, annualisation
questions.stem: A callable bond is priced at 101.40. A valuation model shows that the price would be 104.30 if the benchmark yield curve fell by 50 bps and 98.60 if it rose by 50 bps (both after allowing for the call option). The bond's effective duration is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. Effective duration = (V− − V+) / (2 × V0 × ΔCurve) = (104.30 − 98.60) / (2 × 101.40 × 0.005) = 5.70/1.0140 = 5.62.

A is incorrect. 11.24 omits the 2 in the denominator, so the price change over the whole 100 bp range is divided by a 50 bp shift and the result is doubled.

C is incorrect. 2.81 uses the full 100 bp range (1%) as the curve shift and also keeps the 2, so it is halved.

BA II Plus: (104.30 − 98.60) ÷ (2 × 101.40 × 0.005) = 5.6213. Use brackets, or compute the denominator first and store it.

questions.concept: Duration/convexity concepts: effective vs modified, empirical, price-yield asymmetry, horizon and reinvestment risk
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about duration and convexity is least accurate?

options.A: The Macaulay duration of a zero-coupon bond equals its time to maturity.
options.B: Modified duration, unlike effective duration, reflects changes in a bond's expected cash flows caused by embedded options when benchmark yields change.
options.C: For two bonds with the same duration and yield, the bond with the higher convexity gains more when yields fall and loses less when yields rise.

questions.explanation:
B is correct (it is the inaccurate statement). It is reversed. Modified duration is based on the bond's yield to maturity and assumes the cash flows do not change when yields change. Effective duration is based on a full valuation model and the benchmark curve, so it captures how option exercise changes expected cash flows. That is why effective duration is the appropriate measure for callable and putable bonds.

A is incorrect (accurate statement). A zero-coupon bond has a single cash flow at maturity, so its weighted-average time to receipt is its maturity.

C is incorrect (accurate statement). Higher convexity means the price-yield curve bends more, so for equal yield changes the price gain is larger and the price loss smaller. This is the price-yield asymmetry that the convexity adjustment captures.

LOS idea: effective vs modified duration; Macaulay duration of a zero; convexity.

questions.concept: Duration/convexity concepts: effective vs modified, empirical, price-yield asymmetry, horizon and reinvestment risk
questions.stem: An investor with a 6-year investment horizon buys a bond with a Macaulay duration of 6.0 years at a yield to maturity of 5%. Immediately after purchase, yields rise by 100 bps in a one-time parallel shift and stay at the new level. All coupons are reinvested at the new yield and the bond is sold at the horizon. Compared with the 5% yield to maturity at purchase, the investor's annualised horizon return will most likely be:

options.A: approximately equal, because the price loss at the horizon is offset by the gain from reinvesting at a higher rate.
options.B: significantly lower, because the capital loss from the higher yield exceeds the extra income earned by reinvesting coupons.
options.C: significantly higher, because the investor's horizon is shorter than the bond's maturity, so the price decline is irrelevant to the return.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. When the Macaulay duration equals the investment horizon, interest rate (price) risk and reinvestment risk offset each other for a one-time parallel yield shift. The rise in yield lowers the sale price but raises reinvestment income by about the same amount, so the realised return is approximately the original YTM.

B is incorrect. It counts the price loss but ignores the offsetting reinvestment gain. With a horizon shorter than the maturity the investor is exposed to both effects.

C is incorrect. Because the bond is sold at the horizon, before maturity, its price at that time reflects the higher yield; the price decline is relevant. It is the offset with reinvestment income that keeps the return near 5%.

LOS idea: Macaulay duration = horizon immunises against a parallel shift; horizon return and reinvestment risk.

questions.concept: Spot, forward and par rates: implied spot from forwards, forward from spots
questions.stem: The 1-year spot rate is 2.0%, the 1-year forward rate one year from now (1y1y) is 3.0%, and the 1-year forward rate two years from now (2y1y) is 4.5%. All rates are annual with annual compounding. The 3-year spot rate is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. (1 + S3)3 = (1 + S1)(1 + f1,1)(1 + f2,1) = 1.02 × 1.03 × 1.045 = 1.0979. S3 = 1.09791/3 − 1 = 3.16%.

A is incorrect. 3.75% is the average of the two forward rates (3.0% and 4.5%); it omits the 1-year spot rate and is not a geometric calculation.

B is incorrect. 4.78% takes the square root instead of the cube root: the product covers three annual periods, so the exponent must be 1/3.

BA II Plus: 1.02 × 1.03 × 1.045 = 1.0978; [yx] 3 [1/x] = 1.0316; − 1 = 0.0316 (3.16%).

questions.concept: Spot, forward and par rates: implied spot from forwards, forward from spots
questions.stem: The 2-year spot rate is 3.2% and the 5-year spot rate is 4.1%, both annual rates with annual compounding. The implied 3-year forward rate two years from now (2y3y) is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. (1 + S2)2(1 + f2,3)3 = (1 + S5)5. So f2,3 = [(1.041)5 / (1.032)2]1/3 − 1 = [1.1479]1/3 − 1 = 4.70%.

A is incorrect. 2.80% takes the fifth root of the ratio, as if the forward period lasted 5 years; the forward covers only the last 3 years (years 3 to 5).

C is incorrect. 4.93% divides the 3-year growth (1.1479 − 1) by 3, an arithmetic average, instead of taking the geometric root.

BA II Plus: 1.041 [yx] 5 = 1.2224; ÷ (1.032 [yx] 2) = 1.1479; [yx] 3 [1/x] = 1.0470; − 1 = 4.70%. Use brackets for the denominator.

questions.concept: Yield spreads: G-spread, Z-spread, I-spread, credit spread movement
questions.stem:
A corporate bond with 6.4 years to maturity yields 5.57%. The table shows benchmark yields:

MaturityGovernment yieldSwap rate
5 years3.90%4.10%
7 years4.50%4.60%

Using linear interpolation for the 6.4-year benchmarks, the bond's I-spread is closest to:

options.A: 112 bps
options.B: 125 bps
options.C: 97 bps

questions.explanation:
A is correct. The I-spread is the bond yield minus the interpolated swap rate. Weight on the 7-year point = (6.4 − 5)/(7 − 5) = 0.70. Swap rate = 4.10 + 0.70 × (4.60 − 4.10) = 4.45%. I-spread = 5.57 − 4.45 = 1.12% = 112 bps.

B is incorrect. 125 bps is the G-spread: it uses the interpolated government yield (3.90 + 0.70 × 0.60 = 4.32%) as the benchmark instead of the swap curve.

C is incorrect. 97 bps subtracts the 7-year swap rate (4.60%) rather than interpolating to the bond's 6.4-year maturity.

LOS idea: G-spread uses the government curve, I-spread the swap curve; the Z-spread is a constant spread over the whole spot curve and would require spot rates.

questions.concept: Securitization, MBS/ABS, CMO tranches, SPE, non-recourse loans
questions.stem: A bank securitizes a pool of auto loans by transferring them to a special purpose entity (SPE), which issues tranched asset-backed securities (ABS) to investors. Which of the following statements is least accurate?

options.A: Because the loans are legally sold to the SPE, they are generally beyond the reach of the bank's creditors if the bank becomes insolvent.
options.B: Credit enhancement, such as subordination or overcollateralization, can allow the senior tranche to be rated higher than the originating bank.
options.C: If losses on the loan pool exceed the available credit enhancement, ABS investors have recourse to the bank's other assets.

questions.explanation:
C is correct (it is the inaccurate statement). Securitization is non-recourse to the originator once the true sale is made. Investors rely on the cash flows and collateral in the SPE and its credit enhancement; if losses exceed that protection, they cannot claim against the bank's other assets.

A is incorrect (accurate). A key purpose of the SPE is to make the pool bankruptcy-remote from the originator.

B is incorrect (accurate). Internal credit enhancement (subordination, overcollateralization, excess spread) is what allows the senior tranche to achieve a higher rating than the originator.

questions.concept: Bond features: callable, putable, sinking fund, make-whole, negative covenants, FRN reset
questions.stem: Compared with a bond that is callable at a fixed price after a call-protection period, a bond with a make-whole call provision will most likely:

options.A: be more likely to be called when interest rates decline, because the call price is fixed below par and the issuer can refinance cheaply.
options.B: give the issuer less incentive to call when rates decline, because the call price is the present value of remaining payments at a Treasury yield plus a fixed spread.
options.C: give bondholders less protection against early redemption than a fixed-price call, because the make-whole price can never exceed par.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. The make-whole price discounts the remaining coupons and principal at a benchmark yield plus a small fixed spread. When rates fall, the call price rises, which makes calling the bond expensive and keeps the issuer from refinancing. Make-whole calls are mainly used to allow early redemption (for example in a takeover or restructuring) at a fair price to the bondholder.

A is incorrect. The make-whole price is not set below par; when rates fall it is typically above par, so the incentive to call falls.

C is incorrect. The make-whole price is not capped at par; it is the PV of the remaining cash flows and normally exceeds par, protecting bondholders.

questions.concept: Credit analysis: leverage ratios, notching, expected loss, seniority
questions.stem: A bank has an exposure of USD 8,000,000 to a corporate borrower. The estimated probability of default over the next year is 2.5% and, if default occurs, the bank expects to recover 55% of the exposure. The bank's expected loss is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. Expected loss = PD × LGD × exposure. LGD = 1 − recovery rate = 45%. EL = 0.025 × 0.45 × 8,000,000 = USD 90,000.

B is incorrect. USD 110,000 multiplies by the recovery rate (55%) instead of the loss given default (45%).

C is incorrect. USD 200,000 is PD × exposure; it assumes nothing is recovered (LGD of 100%).

BA II Plus: 8,000,000 × 0.025 × (1 − 0.55) = 90,000.

questions.concept: Money market yields and BEY: discount vs add-on
questions.stem: A 180-day Treasury bill is quoted at a discount rate of 3.60% (360-day year basis). The bond equivalent yield (365-day year, simple annualisation) is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. Price per 1 of face = 1 − 0.036 × 180/360 = 0.9820. Holding period return = (1 − 0.9820)/0.9820 = 1.8330%. Bond equivalent yield = HPR × 365/180 = 3.72%.

A is incorrect. 3.67% is the add-on yield on a 360-day year (HPR × 360/180). The bond equivalent yield uses 365 days.

B is incorrect. 3.75% is the effective annual yield, (1 + HPR)365/180 − 1. It compounds, whereas the bond equivalent yield is a simple annualisation.

BA II Plus: 1 − 0.036 × 180 ÷ 360 = 0.982; 1 ÷ 0.982 − 1 = 0.018330; × 365 ÷ 180 = 0.03717.

questions.concept: Term structure: yield curve shapes and theories
questions.stem: An analyst believes investors expect short-term interest rates to remain unchanged, yet the government yield curve is upward sloping. Which of the following statements best explains the upward slope under the liquidity preference theory?

options.A: Forward rates equal expected future spot rates, so the upward slope reflects only expected future increases in short-term rates.
options.B: Investors demand a premium for holding longer bonds, so forward rates exceed expected future spot rates by a premium that grows with maturity.
options.C: Supply and demand in each maturity segment are independent, so the slope is unrelated to expected future short-term rates or premiums.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Liquidity preference theory adds a liquidity (term) premium to the pure expectations theory. Even with flat expected short rates, the premium rises with maturity, so the curve slopes upward.

A is incorrect. This describes the pure expectations theory, under which unchanged expected short rates would produce a flat curve.

C is incorrect. This describes the market segmentation theory, which attributes the shape to supply and demand in separate maturity segments, not to a liquidity premium.

questions.concept: Issuance and trading: primary market, shelf registration, covered bonds, repo mechanics
questions.stem: A dealer enters a 45-day repurchase agreement to raise cash. It delivers collateral with a market value of CHF 12,000,000. The haircut is 5% and the repo rate is 2.4% (360-day year). The amount the dealer must pay to repurchase the collateral at maturity is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. The haircut reduces the cash lent: loan = 12,000,000 × (1 − 0.05) = CHF 11,400,000. Interest = 11,400,000 × 0.024 × 45/360 = 34,200. Repurchase price = CHF 11,434,200.

B is incorrect. CHF 12,036,000 applies the repo rate to the full collateral value, as if the dealer received CHF 12,000,000; the haircut means the dealer borrows less than the collateral is worth.

C is incorrect. CHF 11,462,857 computes the loan as collateral value / 1.05 (treating the haircut as a markup) rather than collateral × (1 − haircut).

BA II Plus: 12,000,000 × 0.95 = 11,400,000; × (1 + 0.024 × 45 ÷ 360) = 11,434,200.

questions.concept: Indenture and legal structure: secured vs unsecured, zero and deferred coupon
questions.stem: An issuer sells two 10-year bonds with annual coupons, both priced to the same yield to maturity of 5.5%. Bond X pays a 5% coupon starting in year 1. Bond Y pays no coupon in years 1 to 3 and then pays the same 5% coupon in years 4 to 10. Both repay par at maturity. Relative to Bond X, Bond Y will most likely have a:

options.A: lower price and a shorter duration.
options.B: higher price and a longer duration.
options.C: lower price and a longer duration.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. Bond Y is a deferred-coupon bond and forgoes three coupons, so at the same yield its present value is lower (about 82.74 vs 96.23 per 100). Because more of its value comes from later cash flows (the coupons paid in years 4 to 10 and the principal), the weighted-average time to receipt is longer: Macaulay duration is about 9.06 years vs 8.07 years for Bond X.

A is incorrect. The price is lower, but removing early cash flows lengthens, not shortens, the duration.

B is incorrect. Bond Y receives fewer cash flows, so its price cannot be higher at the same yield.

questions.concept: Yield-to-worst, horizon return, key-rate duration
questions.stem: A bond has 8 years to maturity and pays a 7% coupon semiannually. It is priced at 108.50 per 100 of par on a coupon date. The bond can be called in 3 years at 103. Yields are stated as annual rates compounded semiannually. The bond's yield to worst is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. A bond trading at a premium is most likely to be called, so compare the yield to maturity and the yield to call. YTM: N = 16, PMT = 3.5, FV = 100, PV = −108.50 gives 5.66%. YTC: N = 6, PMT = 3.5, FV = 103, PV = −108.50 gives 2.4309% per period = 4.86%. The yield to worst is the lowest of the possible yields: 4.86%.

A is incorrect. 5.66% is the yield to maturity. A premium bond with a call date has a lower yield to call, which is the worst case for the investor.

C is incorrect. 3.97% uses a call price of 100 instead of the stated 103, which understates the cash received at the call and the yield to call.

BA II Plus: 6 [N], 3.5 [PMT], 103 [FV], −108.5 [PV], [CPT] [I/Y] = 2.4309; × 2 = 4.86%. (Remember N = years × 2 and multiply the periodic yield by 2.)

questions.concept: Prepayment measures: CPR, PSA, extension and contraction
questions.stem: A pool of mortgages is prepaying at 150 PSA. The conditional prepayment rate (CPR) assumed in month 10 is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. The 100 PSA benchmark ramps CPR from 0 by 0.2% per month up to 6.0% at month 30. In month 10, 100 PSA CPR = 6% × 10/30 = 2.0%. At 150 PSA the CPR is 1.5 times that: 2.0% × 1.5 = 3.0%.

B is incorrect. 9.0% = 6% × 1.5 applies the fully seasoned CPR, ignoring that month 10 is still in the ramp-up period.

C is incorrect. 2.0% is the CPR at 100 PSA in month 10; the 150% multiple was not applied.

LOS idea: PSA benchmark; faster prepayments (higher PSA) shorten average life (contraction), slower ones lengthen it (extension).

questions.concept: Sovereign and municipal issuers: credit analysis and funding choices
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about sovereign credit analysis is least likely to be accurate?

options.A: The strength of a country's institutions, such as rule of law and predictability of policy, is a factor in sovereign credit analysis.
options.B: A sovereign's foreign-currency debt is typically rated higher than its local-currency debt, because foreign investors hold it.
options.C: A government that issues debt in its own currency generally has more flexibility to service that debt than one issuing in a foreign currency.

questions.explanation:
B is correct (it is the inaccurate statement). Local-currency debt is usually rated equal to or higher than foreign-currency debt, because the government can tax and, at the extreme, create its own currency to meet local obligations. It cannot print a foreign currency.

A is incorrect (accurate). Institutional effectiveness and political risk are core sovereign credit factors.

C is incorrect (accurate). Revenue and debt in the same currency removes currency mismatch and adds monetary policy flexibility.

questions.concept: Corporate bond market structure and ratings agencies
questions.stem: Rating agencies often rate the senior unsecured bonds of a holding company one or more notches below the senior unsecured bonds of its operating subsidiary. This notching most likely reflects differences in:

options.A: the liquidity of the bonds in the secondary market, which is usually lower for holding company issues, and the resulting yield premium.
options.B: the probability of default only, because the holding company usually issues more debt than the subsidiary does, which raises its leverage.
options.C: expected recovery if default occurs, because holding company creditors rank behind the subsidiary's own creditors for subsidiary assets.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. Notching adjusts the issuer rating for differences in loss given default. Holding-company creditors are structurally subordinated: subsidiary creditors are paid from subsidiary assets first, so recovery is expected to be lower and the bonds are notched down.

A is incorrect. Ratings measure credit risk (probability of default and loss severity), not secondary market liquidity.

B is incorrect. Notching is mainly about relative recovery, not just default probability, and the amount of debt issued does not by itself explain it.

questions.concept: Put-call parity and put-call-forward parity (c - p direction, PV(X) vs spot)
questions.stem:
European call and put options on Aldine Corp stock have the same strike, USD 50.00, and expire in six months. The stock trades at USD 48.00, the call at USD 3.80, and the annual risk-free rate is 4.0% (annual compounding). The stock pays no dividends.

The put price is closest to:

options.A: USD 4.83
options.B: USD 5.80
options.C: USD 2.77

questions.explanation:
Put-call parity: c + PV(X) = p + S0, so p = c + PV(X) − S0.

PV(X) = 50/1.040.5 = 49.03. p = 3.80 + 49.03 − 48.00 = USD 4.83.

BA II Plus: 1.04 [yx] 0.5 [=] [1/x] [×] 50 [=] 49.03; then 3.80 + 49.03 − 48 = 4.83.

LOS: put-call parity (c − p = S − PV(X)).

Why the others are wrong

  • B — USD 5.80 uses X undiscounted: 3.80 + 50 − 48.
  • C — USD 2.77 flips the direction (p = c − PV(X) + S): 3.80 − 49.03 + 48. Remember c − p = S − PV(X), so p = c − S + PV(X).

questions.concept: Put-call parity and put-call-forward parity (c - p direction, PV(X) vs spot)
questions.stem:
A European call and put on a stock have strike USD 100.00 and expire in one year. The stock trades at USD 90.00 and will pay a dividend before expiry; the one-year forward price on the stock is USD 92.40. The risk-free rate is 5.0% (annual) and the call trades at USD 4.10.

The put price consistent with put-call-forward parity is closest to:

options.A: USD 9.34

questions.explanation:
Put-call-forward parity: c + PV(X) = p + PV(F0(T)), so p = c + [X − F0(T)]/(1 + r)T.

p = 4.10 + (100 − 92.40)/1.05 = 4.10 + 7.238 = USD 11.34.

BA II Plus: 100 [−] 92.4 [÷] 1.05 [+] 4.1 [=] 11.34.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — USD 9.34 uses the spot-based formula p = c + PV(X) − S0 = 4.10 + 95.24 − 90, which ignores the dividend that is embedded in the forward price. With a dividend, spot parity needs S0 − PV(dividend).
  • C — USD 11.70 does not discount the difference: 4.10 + (100 − 92.40).

questions.concept: Option payoffs and profit: long/short call and put, exercise value, time value, protective put, risk reversal
questions.stem: An investor buys a share at USD 50.00 and, at the same time, buys a put on it with a strike of USD 48.00 for a premium of USD 2.50. At expiry the share price is USD 41.00. The profit per share on the protective put position is closest to:
questions.explanation:
At expiry: share worth 41.00; put payoff = 48 − 41 = 7.00. Total value = 48.00 (the floor X). Cost = 50 + 2.50 = 52.50. Profit = 48.00 − 52.50 = −USD 4.50 (= −(S0 − X + p), the maximum loss).

Why the others are wrong

  • A — −2.50 is just the premium; the loss on the share is ignored.
  • B — −11.50 is the share loss (−9) plus premium (−2.50), ignoring the put payoff of 7.

questions.concept: Option payoffs and profit: long/short call and put, exercise value, time value, protective put, risk reversal
questions.stem: An investor establishes a risk reversal on an index: buys a call with strike 105 for USD 2.00 and sells a put with strike 95 for USD 2.60, same expiry. At expiry the index closes at 89. The profit per unit is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Long call (X = 105): worthless at 89. Short put (X = 95): pays out 95 − 89 = 6.00, a loss of 6.00. Net premium = +2.60 received − 2.00 paid = +0.60.

Profit = 0 − 6.00 + 0.60 = −USD 5.40.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — −6.00 ignores the net premium of +0.60.
  • C — −6.60 treats the net premium as a cost (−0.60) although premium received on the put exceeds premium paid on the call.

questions.concept: Forward valuation: mark-to-market, cost of carry, arbitrage direction when F is mispriced
questions.stem:
Six months ago a trader entered a long forward contract to buy a non-dividend-paying stock at USD 102.00 in one year. Today the stock trades at USD 104.00, six months remain, and the risk-free rate is 4.0% (annual compounding).

The current value of the long position is closest to:

options.A: USD 5.92
options.B: USD 3.98
options.C: USD 2.00

questions.explanation:
Vt (long) = St − F0/(1 + r)T−t = 104 − 102/1.040.5 = 104 − 100.02 = USD 3.98.

BA II Plus: 1.04 [yx] 0.5 [=] [1/x] [×] 102 [=] 100.02; 104 − 100.02 = 3.98.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — USD 5.92 discounts the contract price over a full year (102/1.04 = 98.08) instead of the remaining six months.
  • C — USD 2.00 is S − F0 with no discounting.

questions.concept: Forward valuation: mark-to-market, cost of carry, arbitrage direction when F is mispriced
questions.stem: A stock trades at USD 80.00 and will pay a dividend of USD 1.50 in exactly one year. The one-year forward is quoted at USD 81.00. The risk-free rate is 5.0% (annual compounding). Which strategy captures an arbitrage profit and what is that profit at the forward's expiry?

options.A: Buy the forward, short the stock and invest the proceeds; profit USD 1.50
options.B: Sell the forward, buy the stock with borrowed money; profit USD 1.50
options.C: Buy the forward, short the stock and invest the proceeds; profit USD 3.00

questions.explanation:
Fair forward price = S0(1 + r) − dividend = 80 × 1.05 − 1.50 = 82.50. The quoted 81.00 is below fair value (forward underpriced), so buy the forward and short the stock.

At expiry: invested 80 grows to 84.00; pay the stock lender the 1.50 dividend; pay 81.00 under the forward to take delivery and close the short. Profit = 84.00 − 1.50 − 81.00 = USD 1.50 (= 82.50 − 81.00).

Why the others are wrong

  • B — Right profit, wrong direction: selling an underpriced forward and buying the stock locks in a loss.
  • C — Right direction, but 3.00 ignores the dividend owed to the stock lender (84 − 81); fair price is 82.50, not 84.00.

questions.concept: Forwards vs futures: counterparty risk, correlation with rates, open interest, margin and marking to market
questions.stem: A trader buys 5 index futures contracts at 4,000 (multiplier USD 50 per index point). Initial margin is USD 5,000 per contract and maintenance margin is USD 4,000 per contract; the account was funded at exactly the initial margin. At the end of the day the settlement price is 3,970. The amount the trader must deposit to satisfy the margin call is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Daily loss = 30 points × USD 50 × 5 contracts = USD 7,500. Equity = 25,000 − 7,500 = 17,500, below the total maintenance margin of 20,000, so a margin call is made. Variation margin must restore the account to the initial margin of 25,000: deposit USD 7,500.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — USD 2,500 brings equity back only to the maintenance level (20,000 − 17,500); the call requires returning to the initial margin.
  • B — USD 1,500 is the loss per contract (30 × 50); the position has 5 contracts.

questions.concept: Binomial hedge ratio and one-period value; option bounds (min/max European call and put)
questions.stem:
