A dealer has sold 600 one-period European call options, each on one share. The stock is USD 50 and will move to USD 62.50 or USD 40.00 at the end of the period. The strike is USD 55 and the one-period risk-free rate is 5%.

To delta-hedge the position, the dealer should buy approximately:

options.A: 333 shares
options.B: 200 shares
options.C: 1,800 shares

questions.explanation:
Call payoffs: up = 62.50 − 55 = 7.50; down = 0. Hedge ratio h = (c+ − c−)/(S+ − S−) = 7.50/22.50 = 1/3 share per call.

Shares = 600 × 1/3 = 200.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — 333 uses the risk-neutral up-probability π = (1.05 − 0.80)/(1.25 − 0.80) = 0.556 as the hedge ratio.
  • C — 1,800 divides by the hedge ratio (600/0.333) instead of multiplying.

questions.concept: Swaps: swap rate, replication with bonds and forwards
questions.stem: Which statement about a plain vanilla interest rate swap is most accurate?

options.A: A pay-fixed swap is equivalent to issuing a floating-rate bond and investing the proceeds in a fixed-rate bond
options.B: At initiation a swap is typically priced so that its value to the receive-fixed party is positive
options.C: A pay-fixed swap is equivalent to issuing a fixed-rate bond and investing the proceeds in a floating-rate bond

questions.explanation:
The pay-fixed party makes fixed payments (like a fixed-rate issuer) and receives floating payments (like a floating-rate investor): short fixed-rate bond, long floating-rate note. The swap rate is set so that the swap's value is zero to both parties at initiation.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Reverses the legs: that describes the receive-fixed side.
  • B — The swap rate makes the initial value zero for both parties; a positive value would be an off-market swap requiring an upfront payment.

questions.concept: Greeks, implied volatility, derivative uses and risk transfer
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about option sensitivities is LEAST accurate?

options.A: The gamma of a long put is negative because the delta of a put is negative
options.B: The delta of a long call lies between 0 and +1
options.C: All else equal, an increase in implied volatility raises the price of both calls and puts

questions.explanation:
Gamma is the rate of change of delta with respect to the price of the underlying; it is positive for any long option, call or put. A put's delta is negative (between −1 and 0), but that does not make gamma negative: put delta rises toward 0 as the price rises.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — Accurate: call delta is between 0 and 1.
  • C — Accurate: positive vega for long calls and puts.

questions.concept: Futures pricing with income and storage; convenience yield
questions.stem: Crude oil trades at USD 75.00 per barrel. The one-year risk-free rate is 4.0% (annual). The present value of storage costs over the year is USD 2.50 per barrel and the present value of the convenience yield is USD 1.20 per barrel. The no-arbitrage one-year futures price is closest to:
questions.explanation:
F0 = (S0 + PV(storage) − PV(convenience yield))(1 + r) = (75 + 2.50 − 1.20) × 1.04 = 76.30 × 1.04 = USD 79.35.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — USD 80.60 leaves out the convenience yield: (75 + 2.5) × 1.04.
  • C — USD 81.85 adds the convenience yield instead of subtracting it: (75 + 2.5 + 1.2) × 1.04.

questions.concept: Swap valuation after inception; FRA
questions.stem: A two-year annual-pay interest rate swap with notional EUR 50 million has a fixed rate of 3.00%. Current spot rates are 3.2% for one year and 3.6% for two years (annual compounding), and the current par swap rate for the remaining term is 3.593%. The value to the party that pays fixed is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Discount factors: Z1 = 1/1.032 = 0.96899; Z2 = 1/1.0362 = 0.93172. Annuity factor = 1.90071.

Current par swap rate = (1 − 0.93172)/1.90071 = 3.593%.

The payer pays 3.00% when the market rate is 3.593%: a gain of (3.593% − 3.00%) × 50m = 296,457 per year for two years, discounted: 0.005929 × 1.90071 × 50,000,000 = +EUR 563,000.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Sign reversed: that is the value to the receive-fixed party, who is locked into a below-market rate.
  • B — Does not discount the annual savings: 0.005929 × 2 × 50m = 593,000.

questions.concept: Credit derivatives and CDS payoffs
questions.stem: Which statement about a single-name credit default swap (CDS) is most accurate?

options.A: If the reference entity's credit spread widens after initiation, the CDS gains value for the protection buyer
options.B: The protection seller makes periodic premium payments to the protection buyer
options.C: After a credit event the protection buyer pays the seller the difference between par and the recovery value

questions.explanation:
The protection buyer pays the periodic premium (the CDS spread). If the reference entity's credit worsens, the market spread on a new CDS rises, so the existing CDS (which pays protection at the old, lower spread) gains value to the buyer. After a credit event the protection seller pays the buyer the loss, i.e. par minus recovery.

Why the others are wrong

  • B — The buyer pays the premium; the seller receives it.
  • C — Reverses the payer: the seller pays par minus recovery (loss given default) to the buyer.

questions.concept: Exchange-traded vs OTC: clearing, margin, American vs European exercise
questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to describe exchange-traded derivatives?

options.A: Contracts have standardized terms
options.B: Terms such as expiration date and size are tailored to the needs of the counterparties
options.C: A clearinghouse stands between the buyer and seller, reducing counterparty credit risk

questions.explanation:
Tailored terms are a feature of over-the-counter derivatives. Exchange-traded contracts are standardized, trade on a regulated exchange and are guaranteed by a clearinghouse.

Why the others are wrong

  • A — Standardization is a defining feature of exchange-traded contracts.
  • C — The clearinghouse guarantee is a defining feature of exchange-traded contracts.

questions.concept: Private equity and VC: buyout vs growth, exits, MOIC vs IRR, clawback, co-investment
questions.stem: A private equity fund owns a profitable portfolio company. To return capital to the fund without selling its stake, the fund arranges for the company to borrow and pay a large one-time dividend to its shareholders. This transaction is best described as a:

options.A: secondary sale.
options.B: strategic (trade) sale.
options.C: dividend recapitalization.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. In a dividend recapitalization the portfolio company raises new debt and pays the proceeds to its owners, returning cash to the fund while the fund keeps its ownership.

A is incorrect. In a secondary sale the fund sells its stake to another private equity firm or a group of investors, so the fund gives up ownership.

B is incorrect. A strategic (trade) sale is a sale of the company to a corporate buyer, again ending the fund's ownership.

questions.concept: Private equity and VC: buyout vs growth, exits, MOIC vs IRR, clawback, co-investment
questions.stem: Two buyout funds each invest EUR 100 million in a single company at inception and receive a single distribution at exit. Fund P receives EUR 240 million after 9 years. Fund Q receives EUR 180 million after 4 years. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Fund P has the higher IRR because it produces the higher MOIC on the same invested capital.
options.B: Fund Q has the higher IRR despite its lower multiple of invested capital (MOIC), because MOIC ignores the timing of cash flows.
options.C: The IRRs are equal because both funds invested the same amount at inception and exited in a single distribution.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. MOIC = total value / invested capital: Fund P = 2.4×, Fund Q = 1.8×. IRR for a single in and out flow = MOIC1/n − 1: Fund P = 2.41/9 − 1 = 10.2%; Fund Q = 1.81/4 − 1 = 15.8%. Fund Q returned capital sooner, so its IRR is higher.

A is incorrect. A higher MOIC does not imply a higher IRR; MOIC does not consider how long the capital was tied up.

C is incorrect. The same initial investment does not make the IRRs equal; IRR depends on the size and timing of the distributions.

questions.concept: Private equity and VC: buyout vs growth, exits, MOIC vs IRR, clawback, co-investment
questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics would make a company least attractive as a leveraged buyout (LBO) target?

options.A: Highly cyclical earnings and large, unpredictable capital expenditure needs.
options.B: Stable, predictable operating cash flows.
options.C: Substantial tangible assets that can serve as collateral for borrowing.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. An LBO uses a high level of debt that must be serviced from the target's cash flows. Cyclical earnings and heavy, unpredictable capex make those cash flows unreliable and raise the risk of default.

B is incorrect. Stable cash flows are a classic LBO attraction because they support debt service.

C is incorrect. Tangible assets provide collateral, making debt financing easier to obtain.

questions.concept: Fee calculations: hard vs soft hurdle, high-water mark, committed vs invested capital, fund of funds net return
questions.stem: A hedge fund starts the year with USD 200 million of assets and earns a gross return of 14%. The management fee is 1.5% of beginning assets and is deducted first. The incentive fee is 20% of the profit, after the management fee, in excess of a 6% hard hurdle (the hurdle is measured on beginning assets). The return to investors, net of all fees, is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. Gross profit = 14% × 200 = 28.0. Management fee = 3.0. Profit after management fee = 25.0. Hurdle amount = 6% × 200 = 12.0. Excess = 25.0 − 12.0 = 13.0, so the incentive fee = 20% × 13.0 = 2.6. Net profit = 28.0 − 3.0 − 2.6 = 22.4, a net return of 22.4/200 = 11.2%.

A is incorrect. 10.0% applies a soft hurdle: once the hurdle is cleared, the incentive fee is charged on all profit (20% × 25.0 = 5.0). A hard hurdle charges only on the excess over the hurdle.

C is incorrect. 10.9% measures the excess over the hurdle before deducting the management fee (28.0 − 12.0 = 16.0; fee = 3.2); the question states the incentive fee is calculated on profit after the management fee.

BA II Plus: (28 − 3 − 12) × 0.2 = 2.6; (28 − 3 − 2.6) ÷ 200 = 0.112.

questions.concept: Fee calculations: hard vs soft hurdle, high-water mark, committed vs invested capital, fund of funds net return
questions.stem:
A hedge fund charges an incentive fee of 20% of gains above its high-water mark, assessed annually. There is no hurdle rate and no management fee. The net asset value (NAV) per unit starts at USD 100.00, which is the initial high-water mark. Over three years the NAV per unit before incentive fees evolves as follows:

YearNAV per unit before incentive fee
1120.00
2104.00 (after year 1's fee was paid)
3127.00

The incentive fee per unit paid at the end of year 3 is closest to:

options.A: USD 2.20
options.B: USD 1.40
options.C: USD 4.60

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Year 1 fee = 20% × (120 − 100) = 4.00, so NAV after fees = 116.00, which becomes the new high-water mark. Year 2 NAV of 104.00 is below the high-water mark: no fee. In year 3 the fee applies only to the gain above 116.00: 20% × (127.00 − 116.00) = USD 2.20.

B is incorrect. USD 1.40 uses the pre-fee year-1 NAV of 120.00 as the high-water mark. The high-water mark is the NAV after the fee was deducted (116.00).

C is incorrect. USD 4.60 charges on the gain from the year-2 NAV (127 − 104 = 23.00). That recovers the loss and ignores the high-water mark, so investors would pay fees twice on the same gains.

BA II Plus: 120 − 100 = 20 × 0.2 = 4; 120 − 4 = 116; (127 − 116) × 0.2 = 2.2.

questions.concept: Real estate, REITs, infrastructure, MLPs, farmland and timberland features
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about real estate investment trusts (REITs), relative to direct private real estate investment, is most accurate?

options.A: REIT returns are typically less correlated with equity markets, because the underlying properties are appraised infrequently.
options.B: REIT shares always trade at their net asset value, because the underlying properties are professionally appraised.
options.C: REIT shares are generally more liquid, and their prices can trade at a premium or discount to the net asset value of the underlying properties.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. REITs are listed, so their shares trade daily and are far more liquid than direct property. Their market prices are set by supply and demand and can differ from NAV.

A is incorrect. The reverse is true. Because REITs are market priced, their returns are more correlated with equities than appraisal-based private real estate returns, which look smoothed and less volatile.

B is incorrect. Appraisal values give an estimate of NAV, but market prices of REIT shares routinely deviate from it.

questions.concept: Real estate, REITs, infrastructure, MLPs, farmland and timberland features
questions.stem: An investor compares two infrastructure investments. Project X is a toll road that has been planned but not yet built. Project Y is an existing toll road that is already operating. Relative to Project Y, Project X most likely has:

options.A: lower risk, because its revenues carry no demand uncertainty, and a correspondingly lower expected return.
options.B: greater construction and demand risk, a higher expected return, and cash flows starting only after construction.
options.C: immediate and stable cash flows, which give it lower risk but also a higher expected return.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Project X is a greenfield investment (new construction); Project Y is a brownfield (existing) asset. Greenfield projects carry construction, completion and demand-forecast risk and generate no cash flows during the build, so investors require a higher expected return.

A is incorrect. Greenfield projects have more, not less, risk, and demand for a new facility is uncertain.

C is incorrect. This describes a brownfield asset. A project not yet built cannot produce immediate cash flows, and lower risk would not justify a higher expected return.

questions.concept: Hedge fund strategies, lockups, prime broker, fund structures
questions.stem: A hedge fund requires investors to leave their capital in the fund for at least one year after investing. The most likely purpose of this lockup period is to:

options.A: allow the manager to hold less liquid positions without being forced to sell them to meet early redemptions.
options.B: protect the high-water mark by preventing redemptions when the fund's NAV is below it.
options.C: allow the fund to borrow more from its prime broker without receiving margin calls.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. A lockup gives the manager a stable capital base, so illiquid or longer-horizon positions can be held to maturity without fire sales driven by redemptions.

B is incorrect. The high-water mark relates to how performance fees are charged; it does not restrict redemptions and is not the purpose of a lockup.

C is incorrect. Margin requirements are set by the prime broker according to the fund's positions and collateral, not by investors' lockups.

questions.concept: Digital assets: tokens, Bitcoin supply, altcoins vs stablecoins
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about digital assets is least accurate?

options.A: The supply of Bitcoin is capped at 21 million coins by its protocol.
options.B: Stablecoins aim to maintain a stable value by being pegged to a reference asset, often backed by reserves.
options.C: Altcoins are cryptocurrencies whose value is pegged to a fiat currency to reduce price volatility.

questions.explanation:
C is correct (it is the inaccurate statement). Altcoins are all cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin. Stablecoins, not altcoins in general, are the digital assets designed to hold a stable value through a peg.

A is incorrect (accurate). Bitcoin's issuance schedule is limited to 21 million coins.

B is incorrect (accurate). Stablecoins peg to fiat currencies or other assets and are typically backed by reserves.

questions.concept: Commodities: return components, roll yield, contango and backwardation
questions.stem: The futures curve for a commodity is upward sloping (contango). An investor holds long futures positions and rolls them forward as they approach expiration. Assuming the spot price is unchanged, the investor will most likely earn a roll yield that is:

options.A: positive, because the convenience yield exceeds the cost of carry.
options.B: negative, because the costs of storage and financing exceed the convenience yield.
options.C: negative, because the convenience yield exceeds the cost of carry.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Contango arises when storage and financing costs are greater than the convenience yield. Rolling means selling the expiring contract (lower price) and buying a longer-dated one at a higher price, so the roll yield is negative.

A is incorrect. A positive roll yield happens in backwardation, not contango.

C is incorrect. A convenience yield greater than the cost of carry produces backwardation, which gives a positive roll yield; the direction of the reason does not match the sign.

Commodity futures total return = spot return + roll yield + collateral return.

questions.concept: Performance appraisal: TVPI, DPI, RVPI, PME, J-curve
questions.stem: A private equity fund has committed capital of GBP 100 million. To date, investors have paid in GBP 80 million, received distributions of GBP 36 million, and the fund's residual net asset value is GBP 72 million. The fund's TVPI (total value to paid-in) is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. TVPI = (distributions + residual NAV)/paid-in capital = (36 + 72)/80 = 1.35. It equals DPI (36/80 = 0.45) plus RVPI (72/80 = 0.90).

A is incorrect. 0.90 is the RVPI (residual value only). It ignores the distributions already received.

B is incorrect. 1.08 divides by committed capital (100) instead of paid-in capital (80). Paid-in capital is the denominator for TVPI, DPI and RVPI.

BA II Plus: (36 + 72) ÷ 80 = 1.35.

questions.concept: Real estate valuation: cap rate, NOI, appraisal smoothing
questions.stem: An analyst values an office building using the direct capitalization approach with a cap rate of 6.25%. The building's potential gross rental income is CHF 2,400,000 a year. Vacancy and collection losses are 7.5% of potential gross income. Operating expenses (including property taxes and insurance) are CHF 640,000. Annual depreciation is CHF 210,000 and annual mortgage interest is CHF 380,000. The building's estimated value is closest to:

options.A: CHF 25.28 million
options.B: CHF 15.84 million
options.C: CHF 28.16 million

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Effective gross income = 2,400,000 × (1 − 0.075) = 2,220,000. NOI = EGI − operating expenses = 2,220,000 − 640,000 = 1,580,000. Value = NOI / cap rate = 1,580,000/0.0625 = CHF 25,280,000.

B is incorrect. CHF 15.84 million deducts depreciation and mortgage interest. NOI excludes depreciation (non-cash) and financing costs; the cap rate is applied to unlevered income.

C is incorrect. CHF 28.16 million ignores vacancy and collection losses (2,400,000 − 640,000 = 1,760,000) and so overstates NOI.

BA II Plus: 2,400,000 × 0.925 = 2,220,000; − 640,000 = 1,580,000; ÷ 0.0625 = 25,280,000.

questions.concept: Private debt: direct lending, mezzanine, distressed
questions.stem: Compared with senior secured direct loans, mezzanine debt issued by a private company most likely:

options.A: ranks ahead of senior debt in repayment priority but offers a lower yield.
options.B: is subordinated to senior debt, offers a higher yield, and often includes an equity feature such as warrants.
options.C: has a lower expected return and lower risk because it is typically floating rate and covenant heavy.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Mezzanine debt ranks below senior loans (and above common equity), so lenders require a higher return; it often includes equity kickers such as warrants or conversion features, and may pay part of its interest in kind.

A is incorrect. Mezzanine debt is junior to senior debt, not ahead of it.

C is incorrect. Subordination makes mezzanine debt riskier, with a higher, not lower, expected return.

questions.concept: Beta: Cov/sigma_m^2 and rho x sigma_i/sigma_m, then CAPM expected return
questions.stem: The covariance between the returns of Halden Foods and the returns of the market portfolio is 0.0270. The standard deviation of the market portfolio's returns is 18%. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return is 9%. Using the CAPM, the expected return on Halden Foods is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. β = Cov(Ri, Rm) / σm² = 0.0270 / 0.18² = 0.0270 / 0.0324 = 0.8333. E(Ri) = Rf + β[E(Rm) − Rf] = 3% + 0.8333 × 6% = 8.0%.

A is incorrect. 3.9% divides the covariance by σm (0.0270 / 0.18 = 0.15) instead of by the market variance; 3% + 0.15 × 6% = 3.9%.

B is incorrect. 7.5% = 0.8333 × 9% multiplies beta by the whole market return and leaves out the risk-free rate and the market risk premium step.

BA II Plus: 0.18 [x²] = 0.0324 (STO 1); 0.027 ÷ RCL 1 = 0.8333; × 6 + 3 = 8.00.

questions.concept: Beta: Cov/sigma_m^2 and rho x sigma_i/sigma_m, then CAPM expected return
questions.stem: A stock has a correlation of 0.72 with the market portfolio. The standard deviation of the stock's returns is 25% and the standard deviation of the market's returns is 20%. The risk-free rate is 2% and the expected market return is 8%. The stock's expected return under the CAPM is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. β = ρi,m × σi / σm = 0.72 × 25% / 20% = 0.90. E(R) = 2% + 0.90 × (8% − 2%) = 7.4%.

A is incorrect. 5.5% puts the sigmas the wrong way round (ρ × σm / σi = 0.72 × 20 / 25 = 0.576); 2% + 0.576 × 6% = 5.5%. The stock's own σ is the numerator.

C is incorrect. 9.5% drops the correlation (β = 25 / 20 = 1.25); 2% + 1.25 × 6% = 9.5%. That would only be right if the stock were perfectly correlated with the market.

BA II Plus: 0.72 × 25 ÷ 20 = 0.90; × 6 + 2 = 7.40.

questions.concept: SML/CAPM valuation (over/undervalued) and Jensen alpha
questions.stem: A stock has a beta of 1.2. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected return on the market portfolio is 8%. An analyst forecasts an expected return of 8.4% for the stock. Relative to the security market line (SML), the stock is most likely:

options.A: undervalued, with an alpha of +0.6%.
options.B: overvalued, with an alpha of −0.6%.
options.C: overvalued, with an alpha of −4.2%.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Required return = 3% + 1.2 × (8% − 3%) = 9.0%. Alpha = forecast − required = 8.4% − 9.0% = −0.6%. The stock offers less than the SML requires for its beta, so it plots below the SML and is overvalued.

A is incorrect. The magnitude is right but the sign is flipped (required − forecast). A forecast below the required return means overvalued, not undervalued.

C is incorrect. −4.2% multiplies beta by the full market return instead of the risk premium: 3% + 1.2 × 8% = 12.6%; 8.4% − 12.6% = −4.2%. The SML slope is E(Rm) − Rf = 5%, not 8%.

BA II Plus: 8 − 3 = 5; × 1.2 = 6; + 3 = 9.00; then 8.4 − 9 = −0.60.

questions.concept: CAL/CML slope = Sharpe ratio, optimal portfolio, Sharpe vs correlation rule, M-squared
questions.stem: Risky portfolio P has an expected return of 11% and a standard deviation of 16%. The risk-free rate is 3%. An investor combines P with the risk-free asset (borrowing at the risk-free rate if necessary) to build a portfolio with a standard deviation of 24%. The expected return of that portfolio is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. The slope of the capital allocation line is the Sharpe ratio of P: (11% − 3%) / 16% = 0.50. E(R) = Rf + slope × σ = 3% + 0.50 × 24% = 15.0%. Equivalent check: weight in P = 24 / 16 = 1.5, so E(R) = 1.5 × 11% + (−0.5) × 3% = 15.0%.

B is incorrect. 16.5% = 1.5 × 11%: it levers up P but ignores the borrowing cost (the −0.5 weight in the risk-free asset costs 1.5%).

C is incorrect. 18.0% = 1.5 × 11% + 0.5 × 3%: the sign of the borrowing is wrong, so the 1.5% borrowing cost is added instead of subtracted.

BA II Plus: 11 − 3 = 8; ÷ 16 = 0.5; × 24 = 12; + 3 = 15.00.

questions.concept: CAL/CML slope = Sharpe ratio, optimal portfolio, Sharpe vs correlation rule, M-squared
questions.stem: Over the past period a fund returned 12.5% with a standard deviation of 18%. The risk-free rate was 2%. The benchmark market portfolio returned 8% with a standard deviation of 12%. The fund's M² (Modigliani-Modigliani) measure is closest to:
questions.explanation:
A is correct. M² levers or de-levers the fund with the risk-free asset until its risk equals the market's risk, then compares returns. Fund Sharpe ratio = (12.5% − 2%) / 18% = 0.5833. Risk-adjusted fund return = Rf + Sharpe × σm = 2% + 0.5833 × 12% = 9.00%. M² = 9.00% − 8% = 1.00%.

B is incorrect. 9.00% is the risk-adjusted return of the fund. The last step, subtracting the market return, was skipped.

C is incorrect. 9.75% scales the excess return by σp / σm (18 / 12) instead of σm / σp: 2% + 10.5% × 1.5 = 17.75%, less 8% = 9.75%. The fund must be scaled down to market risk.

BA II Plus: 12.5 − 2 = 10.5; ÷ 18 = 0.5833; × 12 = 7.00; + 2 = 9.00; − 8 = 1.00.

questions.concept: Two-asset portfolio sigma (2 w1 w2 rho term), rho = -1 and +1, diversification ratio
questions.stem: A portfolio is invested 60% in Asset X and 40% in Asset Y. Asset X has a standard deviation of 20%, Asset Y has a standard deviation of 30%, and the correlation between the two assets is 0.25. The standard deviation of the portfolio is closest to:
questions.explanation:
B is correct. σp² = wX²σX² + wY²σY² + 2 wX wY ρ σX σY = 0.0144 + 0.0144 + 2(0.6)(0.4)(0.25)(0.20)(0.30) = 0.0144 + 0.0144 + 0.0072 = 0.0360. σp = √0.0360 = 18.97%, about 19.0%.

A is incorrect. 18.0% drops the 2 in the covariance term (cross term 0.0036 instead of 0.0072): √0.0324 = 18.0%.

C is incorrect. 24.0% is the weighted average of the standard deviations (0.6 × 20 + 0.4 × 30). That is the portfolio σ only when ρ = +1; with ρ = 0.25 diversification lowers it.

BA II Plus: 0.6 [x²] × 0.2 [x²] = 0.0144 (STO 1); 0.4 [x²] × 0.3 [x²] = 0.0144 (STO 2); 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.25 × 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.0072; RCL1 + RCL2 + 0.0072 = 0.0360; [2nd][√x] = 0.1897.

questions.concept: Two-asset portfolio sigma (2 w1 w2 rho term), rho = -1 and +1, diversification ratio
questions.stem: Asset A has a standard deviation of 12% and Asset B has a standard deviation of 20%. The correlation between the two assets is −1.0. The weight in Asset A that gives a zero-risk portfolio is closest to:
questions.explanation:
C is correct. With ρ = −1, σp = |wAσA − wBσB|. Setting it to zero: wA(12) = (1 − wA)(20), so wA = 20 / (12 + 20) = 62.5%. Check: 0.625 × 12 = 7.5 = 0.375 × 20.

A is incorrect. 37.5% = 12 / (12 + 20) puts the sigmas the wrong way round. That is the weight A would need if the sigmas were swapped (it is the zero-risk weight of Asset B); it gives |0.375 × 12 − 0.625 × 20| = 8%, not zero. The lower-risk asset needs the larger weight.

B is incorrect. An equal weighting gives |0.5 × 12 − 0.5 × 20| = 4%. Perfect negative correlation does not eliminate risk unless the weights are set to offset the two standard deviations.

BA II Plus: 20 ÷ (12 + 20) = 0.625.

questions.concept: Risk management process: starts with risk tolerance; risk budgeting; governance; VaR meaning
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the risk management process is most accurate?

options.A: Risk governance comes first: it sets the organization's risk tolerance, responsibilities and reporting lines, and the risk budget then allocates the acceptable risk among portfolios or strategies once risks have been identified and measured.
options.B: A risk budget should be set before existing risks are identified and measured, so that measurement can concentrate on budgeted risks.
options.C: Risk governance is the final step, because it documents the exposures that remain after risks have been adjusted.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Risk governance is the foundation: it establishes the framework, responsibilities and risk tolerance under which later steps operate. The organization then identifies and measures its actual risks, allocates acceptable risk through a risk budget, and modifies exposures (avoid, accept, transfer, shift) where actual risk differs from the budget.

B is incorrect. A budget allocates risk against known exposures; it cannot be set sensibly before the existing risks have been identified and measured.

C is incorrect. Governance is the first step, not the last; without it there is no tolerance or accountability framework to guide measurement, budgeting or adjustment.

questions.concept: Risk management process: starts with risk tolerance; risk budgeting; governance; VaR meaning
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about value at risk (VaR) and risk budgeting is least likely accurate?

options.A: A one-day 5% VaR of USD 3.2 million means a loss of at least USD 3.2 million would be expected on about one day in twenty.
options.B: Risk budgeting allocates the total risk an organization is willing to take among its portfolios, strategies or managers, using measures such as VaR or tracking error.
options.C: A one-day 5% VaR of USD 3.2 million is the maximum amount the portfolio can lose on any single day.

questions.explanation:
C is correct (least accurate). VaR is a minimum loss in the worst 5% of outcomes, not a maximum. On the bad 5% of days the loss can exceed USD 3.2 million, and VaR says nothing about how much more. This is why VaR is complemented by stress testing.

A is incorrect (it is accurate). This is the standard interpretation: a 5% probability of a loss of at least the VaR amount over the horizon.

B is incorrect (it is accurate). Risk budgeting divides the overall risk tolerance among units, often in terms of VaR, tracking error or beta, so risk is taken where it is expected to be rewarded.

questions.concept: Risk tolerance (ability vs willingness), risk objectives absolute vs relative, risk aversion
questions.stem: Marta Kowalczyk, 62, tells her adviser she wants to maximize growth and would be comfortable with a 30% fall in her portfolio. Her pension will cover only 40% of her essential spending, and she must draw on this portfolio for the rest within eight years. Her overall risk tolerance is most likely:

options.A: above average, because her willingness to take risk is high.
options.B: average, because high willingness offsets low ability.
options.C: below average, because her ability to take risk is low.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. Risk tolerance has two components: willingness (psychological) and ability (financial capacity: liabilities, time horizon, wealth, other income). Marta's willingness is high but her ability is low: a short horizon, heavy reliance on the portfolio and a pension that covers only part of her needs. When the two conflict, the lower of the two determines overall risk tolerance.

A is incorrect. It relies on willingness alone; willingness cannot create financial capacity to bear losses.

B is incorrect. The components are not averaged. A client who cannot afford a loss should not be exposed to it just because she is willing to accept it.

questions.concept: Behavioral biases: cognitive vs emotional, curable vs not, anomalies explained by bias
questions.stem: Aisha Rahman's fund has fallen 30% since she bought it. Her adviser's analysis shows that selling and switching to a comparable fund would improve her prospects, but Aisha refuses to sell because she 'cannot stand locking in the loss'. This behavior is most likely:

options.A: a cognitive error, best addressed by giving Aisha more information about the fund.
options.B: an emotional bias, which is hard to correct, so the adviser should adapt the advice to the bias where possible.
options.C: an emotional bias, which is easily corrected through education, so the adviser should insist on the sale.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Reluctance to realize a loss is loss aversion, an emotional bias arising from feelings rather than faulty reasoning or information processing. Emotional biases are difficult to override, so the adviser's practical response is to adapt to the bias (for example, a staged switch) rather than try to eliminate it.

A is incorrect. Cognitive errors come from faulty reasoning or memory, and more information and education help correct them. Aisha already has the information; her problem is emotional discomfort.

C is incorrect. The classification is right but the treatment is not: emotional biases are less amenable to correction by education, and insisting on the sale risks the client relationship without removing the bias.

questions.concept: Behavioral biases: cognitive vs emotional, curable vs not, anomalies explained by bias
questions.stem: Researchers find that stocks with the highest returns over the past 12 months continue to outperform over the following 3 to 12 months. Other authors propose that herding and under-reaction to news explain the pattern. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: The pattern remains a market anomaly even though behavioral biases are offered as an explanation.
options.B: The pattern ceases to be an anomaly once a behavioral bias is shown to explain it.
options.C: The pattern is evidence that the market is semi-strong form efficient.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. An anomaly is a persistent pattern in returns that cannot be explained by the efficient market hypothesis and a rational risk-based model. Proposing that behavioral biases (herding, under-reaction) cause the pattern gives an explanation for why it exists, but the pattern is still inconsistent with efficient markets and is still an anomaly.

B is incorrect. A behavioral explanation does not remove the anomaly; it reconciles the pattern with behavioral rather than rational models.

C is incorrect. Predictable outperformance based on past prices contradicts even the weak form, so it cannot support semi-strong efficiency.

questions.concept: IPS, investor types and pooled funds, active vs passive
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about institutional investors is least likely accurate?

options.A: A defined-benefit pension plan with mostly retired members typically has a shorter time horizon and greater liquidity needs than one with mostly young members.
options.B: An endowment typically has a perpetual time horizon, and its return objective usually has to cover spending needs plus inflation.
options.C: Property and casualty insurers typically have longer and more predictable liabilities than life insurers and can therefore hold more illiquid assets.

questions.explanation:
C is correct (least accurate). It is the reverse of the true position. Life insurers have long-term, relatively predictable liabilities and can hold longer, less liquid assets. Property and casualty insurers face shorter, less predictable claims, so they need more liquid, shorter-duration portfolios.

A is incorrect (it is accurate). A mature plan pays out sooner and has less time to recover from losses, so its horizon is shorter and its liquidity needs higher.

B is incorrect (it is accurate). Endowments aim to preserve real capital for future generations while funding current spending, so the required return is approximately spending rate plus inflation.

questions.concept: Risk aversion and utility; HPR and indifference curves
questions.stem:
An investor has a risk aversion coefficient A = 4 and uses the utility function U = E(R) − 0.5 A σ². She is choosing among three portfolios:

PortfolioE(R)σ
X10.0%18%
Y8.5%12%
Z5.5%5%

The portfolio that gives her the highest utility is:

options.A: Portfolio X.
options.B: Portfolio Y.
options.C: Portfolio Z.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. UX = 0.100 − 0.5(4)(0.18)² = 0.100 − 0.0648 = 0.0352. UY = 0.085 − 2(0.0144) = 0.085 − 0.0288 = 0.0562. UZ = 0.055 − 2(0.0025) = 0.055 − 0.005 = 0.0500. Y has the highest utility (5.62%).

A is incorrect. X has the highest expected return but its risk penalty (6.48%) is so large that its utility is only 3.52%. Choosing the highest return ignores risk aversion.

C is incorrect. Z is the choice of someone who drops the 0.5 from the penalty term (U = E(R) − Aσ²): Z = 0.055 − 0.010 = 0.045 beats Y = 0.085 − 0.0576 = 0.0274. With the correct formula Z scores 5.00%, below Y.

BA II Plus: for Y: 0.12 [x²] = 0.0144; × 2 = 0.0288; 0.085 − 0.0288 = 0.0562.

questions.concept: IPS constraints (liquidity, horizon, tax, legal, unique); strategic vs tactical allocation
questions.stem: An adviser is classifying the constraints in three clients' investment policy statements (IPS). Which of the following classifications is most likely correct?

options.A: A client refuses to hold tobacco companies on moral grounds: legal and regulatory constraint.
options.B: A client's capital gains are taxed more heavily than dividend income: unique circumstances.
options.C: A client needs GBP 180,000 in 15 months to buy a business: liquidity constraint.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. A known, near-term cash need is the classic liquidity constraint: part of the portfolio must be held in assets that can be sold quickly at close to their value.

A is incorrect. A personal ethical preference is a unique circumstance. Legal and regulatory constraints come from external laws, rules and trust or regulatory requirements, not from the client's values.

B is incorrect. Different tax rates on capital gains and dividends are a tax constraint, affecting after-tax returns and the choice between income and growth assets. Unique circumstances cover things such as ESG exclusions or a concentrated inherited holding.

LOS idea: the five IPS constraint categories: liquidity, time horizon, tax, legal and regulatory, unique circumstances.

questions.concept: Treynor ratio, systematic vs unsystematic risk, efficient frontier
questions.stem:
The risk-free rate is 3%. Two well-diversified portfolios have the following results:

PortfolioReturnBetaStandard deviation
P12.0%1.2020%
Q10.5%0.8022%

Which portfolio ranks higher on each measure?

options.A: Treynor ratio: P; Sharpe ratio: Q.
options.B: Treynor ratio: Q; Sharpe ratio: P.
options.C: Treynor ratio: P; Sharpe ratio: P.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Treynor = (Rp − Rf) / β: P = 9.0 / 1.20 = 7.50%; Q = 7.5 / 0.80 = 9.375%, so Q is higher. Sharpe = (Rp − Rf) / σ: P = 9.0 / 20 = 0.450; Q = 7.5 / 22 = 0.341, so P is higher. The rankings differ because Treynor rewards systematic risk only (Q has much lower beta) while Sharpe uses total risk.

A is incorrect. This swaps the denominators: it ranks by Sharpe what is Treynor and vice versa (using σ to compare Treynor and β to compare Sharpe).

C is incorrect. P wins on Sharpe but not on Treynor. P's higher raw excess return (9.0% vs 7.5%) is overwhelmed by its higher beta when divided by beta.

BA II Plus: 12 − 3 = 9; ÷ 1.2 = 7.50. 10.5 − 3 = 7.5; ÷ 0.8 = 9.375; 9 ÷ 20 = 0.450; 7.5 ÷ 22 = 0.341.

questions.concept: Portfolio management process (plan, execute, feedback); ETFs and hedge funds as products
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about pooled investment products and management styles is least likely accurate?

options.A: Hedge funds are typically subject to the same leverage and short-selling restrictions as mutual funds sold to the public.
options.B: ETF shares trade on an exchange at intraday prices, and the creation and redemption process used by authorized participants helps keep the price close to net asset value.
options.C: Passive management seeks to replicate a benchmark and typically charges lower fees than active management.

questions.explanation:
A is correct (least accurate). Hedge funds are lightly regulated private pools. They can use leverage, short selling and derivatives, usually charge performance fees, and may impose lock-ups. Public mutual funds face much tighter limits on leverage and short selling.

B is incorrect (it is accurate). Unlike open-end mutual funds, which transact at end-of-day NAV, ETFs trade intraday, and arbitrage by authorized participants keeps price near NAV.

C is incorrect (it is accurate). Passive strategies track an index with little research cost and low turnover, so fees are lower than for active strategies.

questions.concept: Risk modification (insulate, transfer, shift) and stress testing
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about risk modification and stress testing is most accurate?

options.A: Stress tests apply extreme but plausible scenarios to a portfolio and can reveal losses that a VaR estimate based on normal market conditions would understate.
options.B: Buying an insurance policy is an example of risk shifting, whereas using derivatives to change the distribution of outcomes is risk transfer.
options.C: Stress testing assigns a probability to each scenario, so its results can be used in place of VaR.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. Stress testing and scenario analysis examine portfolio outcomes under extreme historical or hypothetical events. They complement VaR, which describes losses under normal conditions and says nothing about the size of losses beyond the VaR threshold.

B is incorrect. The labels are swapped. Insurance is risk transfer (the risk passes to a third party for a premium). Using derivatives to change the probability distribution of outcomes is risk shifting.

C is incorrect. Stress tests do not attach probabilities to the scenarios, which is a limitation; they supplement VaR and cannot replace it.
